speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-130, to amend the Canada Grain Act (rape-seed and mustard seed).

subtopic: REVISION OF GRADES RESPECTING RAPESEED AND MUSTARD SEED
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: REVISION OF GRADES RESPECTING RAPESEED AND MUSTARD SEED
speechtext:
Canada, Mr. Speaker, is best known in the commercial markets of the world for the high quality of its grain, particularly wheat. The purpose of this bill to amend the Canada Grain Act is to bring other grains such as rapeseed and mustard seed to the same high standard. Ninety to 95 per cent of all the rapeseed grown in this country is exported, and it is imperative that the quality of this grain be of the highest standard that we are able to achieve for it.
The amendment proposes to revise the present statutory grades for rapeseed to meet

Inquiries of the Ministry present-day trade requirements. This is in conformity with the suggestion of the board of grain commissioners for Canada to have the Canada Grain Act reclassified in accordance with attached schedules A and B. It also meets with the full approval of the Minister of Agriculture, under whose jurisdiction the Canadian wheat board and the board of grain commissioners for Canada come, and I am sure it will also meet with the approval of hon. members of the House of Commons. Schedules A and B are based on the recommendation of the chief grain inspector for the board of grain commissioners for Canada, and are in compliance with the export requirements, containing stipulations with regard to maximum percentage of foreign materials, degree of soundness and standard of cleanliness.
Clause 2 of the bill will change the definition of the grades of domestic mustard seed from the present commercial definition to a statutory definition. The committee on western grain standards established commercial grades for domestic mustard seed on November 4, 1953. These grades have now been revised to meet trade requirements, and the effect of this amendment is to raise these revised commercial grades to the precedence of statutory grades.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF ADVISORY COUNCIL ON FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Monteith (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF ADVISORY COUNCIL ON FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure respecting the encouragement of fitness and amateur sport in Canada; to provide for the making of grants to agencies, organizations or institutions; to provide for entering into an agreement with any province for the payment by Canada to the province of certain contributions in respect of the costs of programs relating to fitness and amateur sport; to provide for the establishment of a council to be called the national advisory council on fitness and amateur sport; to provide for the payment of the chairman's remuneration and of the travelling and other expenses of the members of the council; and to provide further that the Minister of Finance shall pay out of the consolidated revenue fund each fiscal year such amounts not exceeding in the aggregate five million dollars as may be required for the purposes set forth in the measure.
Motion agreed to, and the house went into committee, Mr. Chown in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF ADVISORY COUNCIL ON FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to introduce this measure relating to fitness and amateur sport, the intent of which was announced by the Prime Minister recently in Toronto. Particularly at this time when our thoughts are so much taken up with the sombre threat to our way of life, and indeed to human existence itself, it is refreshing and heart warming to turn to a matter which is wholly dedicated to the greater benefit and enjoyment of the people of Canada.
As hon. members are aware, the resolution now before the committee had its immediate origin in the throne speech of last November. The thinking behind these proposals is not, however, of so recent origin; it dates back several years and, in fact, includes the efforts of a number of hon. members of this house. These and others have been outspoken champions of fitness and amateur sport and have repeatedly urged some form of assistance from the dominion government in support of such activities. While it has not been

possible to implement all their specific suggestions, I hope they will find in our new proposals the achievement of at least the spirit of their intentions.
It is, of course, no secret that the dominion government has previously made efforts in supporting a nation-wide program of physical fitness, and that these proved disappointing. But the fact that the program which was in force from 1943 to 1954 failed to meet expectations does not, to my mind, imply that the job cannot be done, that a new start should not be made. Indeed, as I will be pointing out later when the bill is before the house, circumstances have changed radically in the interval, and moreover, we are convinced that the present plans constitute a very substantial improvement over those previously in effect.
In outlining the background of this measure, mention should be made of the speech delivered by His Royal Highness the Duke of Edinburgh before the Canadian medical association on June 30, 1959. On that occasion, the committee will recall, His Royal Highness drew attention with great force to the extent of what he termed "sub-health" among Canadians. He said:
There is evidence that despite everything, people in Canada are not as fit as they might he-
Then he went on to say:
Some scheme, therefore, which exists to encourage participation in all sports and recreations, for all ages and sections of the community is absolutely essential to any modern community with a high standard of living.
Whether it was the words themselves, or their source, or a combination of both plus a particularly favourable climate of opinion, there can be no doubt that this address by the Duke of Edinburgh had a far reaching impact on Canadian thinking. Certainly an important contributing factor to the en-thusiam of the response on the part of Canadians was what His Royal Highness referred to as "the question of national prestige in sports and games." As he stated quite bluntly:
With a few notable exceptions, Canada's achievements in this line are hardly in keeping with a country which claims almost the highest standard of living in the world.
In any event, with this added stimulus the already growing interest in fitness and amateur sport, which as I have mentioned was highlighted by various members of this house, underwent a sharp upsurge throughout the country. Associations and organizations active in the field as well as the national sports governing bodies began to take on added drive and vitality.
The Canadian Medical Association, which had been the immediate recipient of the Duke

of Edinburgh's challenge, stepped up its consideration of the problem. This bore fruit early in 1961 in the conference on physical fitness sponsored by the Canadian Medical Association in collaboration with its fellow professional organization, the Canadian association for health, physical education and recreation.
The interest of governments also increased. At the provincial level a number of special committees on physical fitness were set up. The committee in Ontario was under the leadership of that distinguished champion of amateur sport, Mr. Harry Price. In the case of the dominion government a new look was taken at the problem with a view to developing an approach which might fit into the current context and which might hold out hope for the achievement of real progress. My department had, of course, continued to maintain consultant services in this field, and had as well set up a special committee to give certain aspects of the subject serious study.
I might point out, incidentally that our reappraisal of the situation has already produced results aside from these present proposals. I refer to the provision of financial assistance through the municipal winter works program for the construction of recreational facilities, as well as the federal grant to the Canadian Olympic Association to further its efforts in obtaining for Canada the 1968 winter Olympics.
In attempting to draw up a new approach to fitness and amateur sport for the long term, we have taken account of a number of basic factors. While the precise relationship between fitness and health remains far from clear, there seems to be no doubt that participation in amateur sport and recreational activities does have a beneficial effect on an individual's well being, particularly with respect to his emotional and social outlook. Besides affording pleasure, participation in competitive games teaches valuable lessons in the exercise of personal powers to the full, in the development of team spirit, and in learning to respect and make friends with one's opponents. The value of these qualities speaks for itself.
Furthermore, in a world which is being constantly reduced more and more to neighbourhood proportions, such qualities can have a vital bearing on the achievement of understanding and friendship among nations and peoples. Indeed, this is where I see the greatest contribution of international competitions. Although we all experience a keen sense of pride and exhilaration when Canadians come out on top in such competitions, I would agree with those who maintain that
Advisory Council on Sports this should not be the overriding consideration. Rather I would go along with the view of Pierre de Coubertin who had much to do with making the Olympic games what they are today. He said:
The important thing is not winning but taking part. The essential thing in life is not conquering but fighting well.
That is the point I believe we should keep before us. Our aim should be primarily to provide the proper environment and training for the youth of Canada so they may in fact be good competitors. If this is done, then we can have every expectation that in due course Canada will have all the champions we could reasonably hope for.
But providing this proper environment and training is not a simple matter these days. Many trends in our society are against it. For example, there is the continuing movement of our people from the more vigorous life of rural areas to large, crowded cities, which too often do not furnish recreational and sports opportunities required by an urban population. Then too the effects of automation have drastically reduced manual labour, and have opened the way for an increasingly sedentary way of life for many Canadians.
These are some of the fundamental factors which we have borne in mind in developing the program which is the subject of the resolution now before the committee. Detailed comments on our new proposals will, of course, have to await presentation of the bill, but there are some general observations which I might make at this stage. As is obvious from the wording of the resolution, the scope of the projected program is broad and comprehensive. The program envisages very generous financial support on the part of the dominion government. Indeed, in setting aside an annual amount of $5 million we are providing greater assistance for fitness and amateur sport than has ever been available in Canada from a single public source.
Moreover, the program does not represent a stereotyped or rigid approach, but provides a framework through which federal aid may be channelled into those areas where it is needed. These include:
1.	The provision of greater assistance to Canadian teams participating in sports meets both at home and abroad.
2.	Support for the expansion of facilities and services for the training of coaches and instructors.
3.	Provision of bursaries and fellowships to improve the competence of personnel connected with fitness and sport.
4.	Support for research and for a greater effort in the field of information.
5.	Granting of fitting recognition for outstanding achievement.

Advisory Council on Sports
As the resolution indicates, federal money will be available for the purposes of the program to agencies, organizations and institutions concerned with fitness and amateur sport. In addition, the proposed measure provides for the development of federal-provincial agreements through which a mutually acceptable arrangement can be worked out for federal assistance designed to strengthen and extend provincial programs in these fields.
In all its many aspects the new plan will benefit from the experience and guidance of a national advisory council which is to be set up under the terms of the legislation. This council will include not more than 30 members representing the provinces and the various agencies concerned with these subjects.
In this connection I should like to emphasize that we do not regard this new program as in any sense a purely federal venture. In the Prime Minister's words, we look on it as a people's program, with all that implies. In other words, not only will its full implementation rest at the grass roots level, but in its development we will welcome the advice and suggestions of all who have an interest in furthering the fitness of the people of Canada, in bringing to our sports activities the qualities that will not only produce champions but will also provide opportunities for as many Canadians as possible to enjoy and benefit from healthy participation in sport and recreational activity.
In referring to this new measure in Toronto recently the Prime Minister formally invited the assistance of any and all Canadians interested in these matters. I am happy to say the response has exceeded all expectations, and I should like to take this opportunity to thank those who have sent us their views. I can assure them that their comments are being given careful study.
In presenting this resolution to the committee today, I should like to follow the Prime Minister's example and say that the government would welcome any suggestions concerning the proposed program which hon. members may wish to put forward. We are very anxious that this be in the fullest sense a bipartisan effort, and to this end I can assure hon. members that their suggestions will be accorded the most serious consideration by the government.
While I would not wish to dampen in any way the enthusiasm aroused by the announcement of this new undertaking, I feel I should issue a word of caution. Although I believe the program to be an excellent one, I do not think we should expect it to achieve miracles overnight. Significant gains will be registered only after a sustained effort, and much remains to be done before such an effort can

be mounted successfully. Progress at first may seem slow, especially if we concentrate on building carefully rather than spectacularly, but we have tremendously improved resources to work with compared to the past.
Given time and patience, I hope we will see great things develop in this field. I hope we will see mounting numbers of our young people engaging in track and field sports, in baseball, hockey, and tennis, to name only a few. I hope we will see adequate facilities for all kinds of sport spring up throughout the length and breadth of Canada. And finally, I hope we will see more and more Canadian athletes achieve that degree of excellence which will make them the equal of the best the world can offer today and in the years ahead.
These are my expectations, Mr. Chairman, as we embark upon an undertaking which I am confident will make a unique contribution to our national development and well-being.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF ADVISORY COUNCIL ON FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, hon. members who heard me speak a couple of years ago on a private member's resolution having to do with this matter will not be surprised when I say that we on this side will support the resolution before the committee. When it is embodied in a bill, Mr. Chairman, we will be glad to accept the minister's invitation to contribute some constructive suggestions which perhaps will improve the bill.
As the minister said, the matter is noncontroversial and I think can be approached in a bipartisan way. It is also, as he pointed out, a resolution which deals with a more cheerful matter than most of those which we have been considering since the house resumed its session.
I must say, Mr. Chairman, that in its original form the resolution was one to which we would have taken exception, but that particular difficulty has been removed by the amendment which was made so that it now reads:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure respecting the encouragement of fitness-
-not through amateur sport, as the first draft of the resolution had it, but the encouragement of fitness and amateur sport in Canada, this is a much better and a much broader way of approaching the problem, as the minister himself pointed out the other day.
Normally there can be a difference between physical fitness and amateur sport. While it may be desirable, and I think it is, for government to accept in this day and age, both on the federal and the provincial levels, some

responsibility in this matter, that responsibility may well be different in its application to physical fitness than to amateur sport.
The resolution itself makes clear that the obligation which the government asks the house to accept in this regard is to be discharged by grants and also-and this is of course very wise-through co-operation with the provinces. Not only must there be, or should there be, co-operation with the provinces, but there must also be, as I think the minister pointed out, the closest kind of cooperation with voluntary bodies concerned with fitness and amateur sport. For this purpose the resolution proposes the establishment of a national advisory council on physical fitness and amateur sport with a paid chairman.
There will be, and there have already been, those in the country who are worried about the entry of the federal government into this field. I have before me an editorial from the Montreal Star of August 29 which gives expression to that worry, arising out of the possibility of government assistance in this field somehow prejudicing the assistance that government should give and has been giving to activities of a non-material kind in other fields. I see no reason why one should in any way interfere with the other, because I think they are both essential.
The editorial which I have just mentioned, expressing this anxiety-and it is an anxiety we ought to keep in mind-has this paragraph:
But even through the vociferous cheering-
The government's announcement has been received with a certain amount of cheering.
-we can hear the subdued voice of the Canadian taxpayer murmuring that he can think of much better ways of spending the money. If anybody put it to him in these terms he would say he would rather see the money go to training minds than bodies.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF ADVISORY COUNCIL ON FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT
speechtext: Let's do both.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF ADVISORY COUNCIL ON FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT
speechtext:
Nobody in this chamber will underestimate at this time the importance of the maximum effort being made by all governments in the training of minds, but surely there is no contradiction between doing perhaps even more than we are doing now for the training of minds, and this initiative to assist in the development of fit bodies through amateur sport and facilities for physical fitness is a step in the right direction. Therefore I do not myself accept any contradiction between these two objectives, although I think there is a danger. If government is not careful it might do more for one than the other, and therefore the balance will have to be preserved. In that balance, of course, I think we would all agree that the training of minds is even more important than the training of bodies.
Advisory Council on Sports
This resolution and the action which will be taken, we hope, through the bill which will be based on it, deal with amateur sport as well as physical fitness. Perhaps we should ask ourselves how government can properly and constructively assist in this field of amateur sport. We might even ask ourselves a question which is not too easy to answer these days. What is amateur sport? The definition of amateur sport in certain instances, and only in certain instances, is such as to take a good deal of the content and meaning out of the word "amateur", and I am sure no one in this house or in the government would wish to direct the kind of assistance for amateur sport which is visualized in this action in a way which would help certain sports bodies train and develop athletes for professional activities when they graduate from some of those amateur bodies.
Then of course amateur sport itself-and I think mention was made of this-has two aspects. There is the domestic aspect and the international aspect. It is perfectly true that the achievements of a nation in amateur athletics, amateur sport, in its domestic aspect leads to achievement in the international side of amateur sport which does do something for a nation's morale, its confidence and its prestige. It may be unfortunate, but it is true that the prestige of a country can be affected by failure in this field, though it should not be nearly as important as failure in other fields. However, in the light of present conditions- all the publicity attached to international sport and the fact that certain societies, particularly the communist societies, use international sport, as they use everything else, for the advancement of prestige and political purposes, it is a matter of some consequence that we in Canada should do what we can to develop and regain the prestige we once had, to a greater extent than we now have in international competition.
The minister mentioned Baron de Coubertin, the founder of the Olympic games and his emphasis, which at least in theory has been the emphasis of the Olympic games ever since, that it is not the achievement but the participation which matters. It is very difficult to maintain that ideal in the face of international competition of the type we have today, even at the Olympic games. Therefore I would hope that an important by-product of assistance, and I think it would only be a by-product, would be to recover in this country most of the prestige that we once had in the field of international athletic competitions.
There was a time not very many years ago when our population was less than half what it is now, when governments did not

Advisory Council on Sports assist international athletic competition, when we did not have the facilities that we have now, let alone the people, when we loomed very large in international competition, especially at the Olympic games. I think I have mentioned before in the house that in 1924 or 1926, I am not sure which, Canada, with not as large a team as she has been able to send to recent Olympic games, managed to win the 100 yards and the 220 yards, and would have won the 440 yards if Jim Ball from Winnipeg had not looked back in the last 10 yards. There is a lesson in that for all of us, not only in athletic competition.
I should hope that the action we are being asked to take now, would do something to encourage the zest for international competition by Canadians, because that is a legitimate and laudable objective, and I think government support of this sort of thing is also legitimate. However, as I said a few minutes ago, the plan has to be very carefully administered indeed; otherwise we may find that our support is going in directions which will not help to achieve the objectives we have in mind. The support can be direct, but I suspect it will be found to be most useful when it is indirect, through helping to finance and develop training facilities and all that kind of thing. Indeed, this is mentioned in the resolution itself.
But government support, however great- I am talking not only about athletics, not only about sport but also about fitness, which is related-will not alone draw young people away from television sets and into games, competition and fitness. There must be in young people that zest for competition, that zest for achievement in games, that desire to go out and take part which I think used to be more noticeable in Canada, when I was young than it is now. We did not have so many distractions at that time, and we were perhaps more concerned with this kind of activity and the good effect it used to have on our fitness and on national morale in those days. All Canadians in those early days got a thrill out of the achievements of our athletes at the Olympic games. I am going back a long way before world war I, when it was taken for granted that if a Canadian did not win the marathon race at the Olympic games he would be among the first two or three, and we had some of the greatest runners of all time in those days.
Perhaps the contrast between that day and now is to be seen in the fact that there is less interest in amateur competition, less interest in games for the sake of playing games, and greater interest in professional competition and in watching professional competition, something about which I should not be


very critical because I spend a good deal of time doing it myself. I think there is also a good illustration in the contrast between our sort of North American approach to these matters and that part of the European approach with which I am familiar. At Oxford University in England-and it is still the same as it was 100 years ago-every day after lunch every student takes part in some form of athletic activity, and if he does not he is considered to be very queer indeed.

only place where that is done.

speechtext:
It is not quite as easy to do that over here, and there is not quite the same incentive. I do not know what is responsible for this change. Perhaps it is a change in our way of life, a change in the habits and customs of the people. I hope that government intervention of this kind may do something to restore what I like to think was an earlier, healthier condition both in games and in fitness. There is no profit in trying to blame anybody or anything. "The fault, dear Brutus, perhaps does not lie in our stars", though the cult of the star may have had something to do with it; and it certainly does not lie in our governments. Rather it lies in ourselves and the situation can be changed if the people wish to change it.
Australia is a good example of what can be done to develop fitness, zest and participation in games without too much government support. There is government support, but that support is not nearly as important as the cooperation that Australian athletes and youth get from voluntary bodies. The same is true in France. There is a good deal of government support in France, and this has a bearing on the danger I mentioned a few moments ago, the danger of perhaps overbalancing support for fitness against support for things of the mind. In France there is more government assistance for the arts, letters and sciences, I suppose, than in any other country in the world-I speak without knowledge of all the facts- and that goes alongside assistance for physical fitness, so the two things are not incompatible.
There is a danger in the government entering this field which I have only touched on so far, the danger that now that the government has taken this responsibility and accepted this obligation there may be a tendency to leave too much to the federal government in what we are now beginning to do. There is also a danger in the administration of a fund of this kind, and we are all aware of that. Who will be helped and how will they be helped? One of the competitions which will develop shortly and for which there will

be a great deal of zest will be the competition to share in this appropriation on the part of all those who think quite rightly that they deserve and need help. Therefore the administration of this fund is going to be very important indeed, and the whole thing can be spoiled by the wrong kind of administration.
I do not need to mention to the minister that it is absolutely essential that there should be completely non-political control over the administration of this fund, as all members will agree, I think, there is in the administration of the funds of the Canada council. The dangers that might arise if this did not happen have been referred to by a good many sports editors who have written some very perceptive articles on the subject matter of this resolution. Jack Kinsella, in the Ottawa Citizen of August 28, 1961, had this to say, and he is in favour of this legislation as I think all sports editors are:
The only thing I don't like about the plan is the inference that it will be politically controlled. Like oil and water, sport and politics don't mix too well.
I have not myself drawn any such inference from the resolution, and I hope none will be required to be drawn. One reason, of course, why the Canada council has this relative independence from political interference is that the council itself is financially independent, in the sense that it derives its income from an endowment. This council, as I understand it, will get its income by means of an annual vote and this, in the nature of things, may result in the loss of such independence as an agency like the Canada council has.
Incidentally, in reference to this question of balance between help for the arts and letters and help for sports and fitness, it is perhaps just as well to remind ourselves that while the amount in this resolution is $5 million a year, that is about twice the income the Canada council gets for all it is trying to do in the field of the arts, letters and sciences. Perhaps the time will come, perhaps it has already come, when the Canada council will make us aware of the fact that this balance will have to be redressed and the council will have to be given more help. The council has already, I believe, made representations in that regard, yet $5 million may soon be considered not enough for all the work that this council may wish to do.
There is an article in the Montreal Star of August 30, 1961 by Baz O'Meara in which he says:
It isn't enough, it should be $25 million.
Of course, Mr. Chairman, it will never be enough.
90205-6-550
Advisory Council on Sports
Then I hope the assistance which is given through this action will be given not to those- I am talking now about the amateur sports side of it-sports which are self sustaining because they are spectator sports. We do not want to help hockey clubs produce professional hockey players or junior football clubs produce professional football players or baseball clubs produce professional baseball players. We do want to help, I think, through the creation of facilities, those sports which will never be self sustaining in the sense that they will be able to meet their expenses. I am thinking of those sports which are extremely important from the physical fitness point of view. I am thinking of aquatic sports and of Ted Reeves' passionate desire to bring lacrosse back to its old place as Canada's national game.
There is one other consideration which I might mention to the committee, and that is the danger which always attaches to this kind of government assistance and actions which are not directly within the field of government activity. I refer to the fact that once this activity becomes dependent to a great extent on government support, then it becomes more difficult to get voluntary assistance for it. The net result would not be good; it would be bad, if these public spirited citizens and organizations in the country who are now interested in amateur sport and fitness felt that now the government had taken over they would not have to do so much; they would not have to produce the funds. I hope it will be made clear that this kind of assistance is a supplement to what people can do for themselves.
This is the danger-perhaps "danger" is too strong a word-as it is apparent in connection with the work of the Canada council. There is a tendency to say the Canada council has this endowment so corporations and wealthy individuals feel they no longer need to contribute. It was the intention of the government in setting up the council to use government support as the foundation on which private enterprise could build its support. However, the temptation is to say, let the government do it; it has taken on this job. I hope this will not happen in connection with this resolution.
Perhaps before I conclude, Mr. Chairman, I might pay my own tribute to those organizations in the country which without very much encouragement in the past have done what they could in this field. I know some of them have become discouraged, but they have worked very hard to improve the physical fitness of our people. I am thinking of Lloyd Percival's sports college, and I am thinking of the central fitness council run by Mr. Harcourt Roy, out in Vancouver, and

Advisory Council on Sports the difficult, rather discouraging work he tried to do to develop physical fitness. I believe he has given up this work and returned to England. There have been people in this country who, in these relatively dark days compared with the brighter days of 25 or 30 years ago in the field of amateur athletics and fitness, have been trying to improve the fitness of the people of this country. This is important work, and the ideal they have in mind is an important ideal; to build up the fitness of our people, not only through amateur athletics but through more direct methods such as those which have been put forward by these two men to whom I have referred.
When the bill is before the house, Mr. Chairman, there will be, as I have said, an opportunity to deal with this matter in detail. However, I am afraid I shall not be able to do so because, as the Prime Minister mentioned, I am going off on a missionary tour shortly in response to the cries of those people who are hungry for the pure gospel. I can only say at this time that we will support the bill and the resolution on which it is based, and we hope that this action by the government will achieve the objective which the government has in mind, of improving the fitness of our people at a time when fitness of the body is only second in importance to fitness of the mind. We hope they will be able to encourage amateur sports generally as a step in the direction of the improvement in physical fitness.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF ADVISORY COUNCIL ON FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT
speechtext:
It is certainly the wish of our party to congratulate the government upon the introduction of this resolution, and especially to congratulate the minister for the very gracious way in which he performed that introduction. This matter is of great interest to all members of this house, as was indicated by the debate on a private member's resolution some months ago. Certainly the interest shown by the hon. member for Kootenay West, who unfortunately had to leave the chamber before he could make his remarks, and by the hon. member for Port Arthur indicates the feeling of our members.
No one questions the purpose of this resolution, nor do we question the need for the bill which will follow, we have no way in which we can obtain accurate statistics as to the level of physical fitness throughout this nation. Over the years we have been receiving some indication from those who are engaged in physical education in the various provinces of Canada that our level is falling behind that which has been achieved in other parts of the world.
A resolution of this nature perhaps raises as many questions as it answers. How do we encourage physical fitness and amateur sports?

How do we encourage physical fitness through amateur sports? It is not the same as subsidizing agriculture or gold mining, because the success of such a program depends on the realization of the material benefits that will be received through the acceptance of the subsidy. Surely the success of this measure is dependent upon the enthusiasm and initiative of the young people or people of all ages who are going to be encouraged to take part in amateur sports, who are going to be encouraged to improve their level of physical fitness.
I am sure each one of us from the various constituencies in Canada has passed playing fields on Saturday afternoon which were completely empty. All of us have heard of schools where they could not find enough boys to play on the football team even though the equipment was there and there was plenty of money available. This is a crucial question; how can a government encourage enthusiasm for physical fitness through legislation?
Another question that arises is this. What group are we mainly concerned with? Are we mainly concerned with young people, or are we really going to try to encourage physical fitness in other age groups? The Leader of the Opposition raised the whole question of what is amateur sport. Can we subsidize amateur sport without the realization that possibly this legislation will be used by professional entrepreneurs for their own benefit as well? The fact is that many sports start out as amateur but end up very much as professional enterprises. Of course the question that arises is this: What sport produces physical fitness to the highest degree and most efficiently? I am sure the minister and his department have dealt with these questions as they bring this resolution to the floor of the House of Commons. Certainly I hope they have done so.
One body which I think has done a great deal in this area is the Central Council of Physical Education in Great Britain, which since 1936 has been trying to deal with the very problem which the minister has brought before us this morning. I should like to read one or two sentences from the 19th annual report of this body:
Our declared aim is: "to promote and improve the physical and mental health of the community through the development of physical recreation". In other words, people are our primary concern, physical recreation-games and sports of all kinds, outdoor activity such as climbing and camping, recreative physical training, dancing and so on- a means to the end.
In other words, let us not regard sports in too narrow a field. The minister mentioned track and field, hockey and football, but let us not simply consider sport as it is

portrayed on the sporting pages of our national newspapers. The results of sports on physical recreation can perhaps be met in many other areas which receive very faint recognition by many sports minded people. Then the report goes on to say this:
The forty or so activities with which we are concerned offer fresh air and exercise to sedentary workers; encourage youngsters to develop their potentialities, to seek adventure and to learn to work and live with others; introduce people of all ages to skills which may give them lifelong pleasure; foster the fuller use and appreciation of the countryside; proffer companionship to the lonely; and guide into constructive channels the energies of those who seek self expression through movement.
Here I think is a very important reflection which the author puts in this last sentence:
But few will voluntarily take part in a physical activity simply because it may "do them good". It must capture their interest, arouse their enthusiasm, make demands on their physical and mental resources-only then will it be really satisfying, really educational.
I would commend those words to the minister and his department because I think this is the crucial point. How do we arouse enthusiasm? How do we arouse initiative?
My greatest fear in connection with this resolution is that we may lose sight of the aim expressed in it. I am sure the Prime Minister did not mean to give this impression, and perhaps I am wrenching this statement out of its context, but when he announced this bill in Toronto he said:
Success in competitive sports ... has become an important element in the contest for the hearts of men. Success in Olympic games and in all fields of international competitive sports has a tremendous effect upon the prestige of nations.
I hope this consideration will not deflect our minds from the main purpose. Reading from an editorial which appeared in an Ontario newspaper, the Peterborough Examiner on August 29, we find concern expressed on the part of this writer who states in one sentence as follows:
If the national advisory council is going to have a brief with overtones of the cold war, we might as well forget about encouragement and take up the Soviet system of compulsory exercises in the factory every day at 11 a.m.
We are certainly interested in the Olympic competitions. However, I think the British council has a point when it says this:
British supremacy in international sport is not the objective of the central council of physical recreation. Yet, the better the council does its work of encouraging everyone, the more probable it is that the country will produce sportsmen of Olympic calibre. Only by broadening the base of the pyramid of participation can its height be increased.
The government in this resolution has chosen three methods by means of which these purposes can be achieved. The first is by 90205-6-550J
Advisory Council on Sports making grants to agencies, organizations or institutions. Of course we hope to see by the bill just exactly what this will mean. However, at this particular moment the matter is all very vague and one is filled with doubts. On what basis is the government going to decide just what are the aims of an organization? Is it really concerned with physical fitness, or does it have other social aims which may entirely undermine the efforts of this agency in carrying out the purpose of this resolution? Before the great rush begins for part of this $5 million, surely a criterion must be established for evaluating the basis on which contributions will be made to these various agencies in order to ensure that the agencies know what amateur sport really is and what its purposes really are.
One person has called it a "slush fund for sport". None of us in this chamber wish to see this take place. However, the national government must take some responsibility for defining with excessive care the kind of sports and activities which will fulfil the aims, the kind of agency which is sincerely motivated to provide physical fitness recreation, which does not have other interest involved and which is concerned also with mass participation.
The second method suggested in this resolution is to provide for entering into an agreement with any province for the payment by Canada to the province of certain contributions in respect of the costs of programs relating to fitness and amateur sport. As we discuss this resolution I am sure we are sobered by the fact that we have already had a physical fitness act. I note that the hon. member for Essex East has just left the chamber. However, before this resolution stage has been completed I hope the hon. member for Essex East, as the former minister of national health and welfare, will give us the benefit of some of his experiences in this field.
Why did that act fail? I spent some time in reading over the minutes of the council from 1943 to 1952 to see whether I could discover why that act had failed to arouse the imagination of the provinces. In 1946 this physical fitness legislation, which was put through by the former administration, was given a citation by the American academy of physical education as pioneering legislation in the interests of human development. Yet by 1953 it had failed. Province after province had not passed physical fitness acts, which I think it had been hoped would be passed. You find rather a sort of ad hoc arrangement by means of which the provinces were attempting to carry out their responsibilities through health and welfare departments, public education departments and so on.

Advisory Council on Sports I was much impressed by the great variety of activities carried on under that physical fitness act in attempting to raise the standard of physical fitness, in attempting to find a role for sports in all parts of Canada, and in attempting to encourage youth through the setting up of physical education departments in our universities. But while I was deeply impressed by what was done, none the less the act failed and it has been wiped off our statute books. In many cases the provinces failed to take up the grants that were available. I note that British Columbia and Saskatchewan seem to have had the most interest in accepting the grants. But certainly as you read through the minutes you could not help but feel that there were major problems. I hope those problems have been looked into by this government, and that they have been dealt with. I noted with some hope a remark by the minister, when he stated that some of the difficulties and concerns in 1961 are different from those of the '40's and '50's. This gives us reason to believe that new initiative in this field will have some effect. I certainly receive the impression that there was a disconcerting lack of trained personnel back in the 1940's and 1950's. With the increase in the physical education branches of our universities, and certainly the far more ambitious program of assistance, we hope that some of these problems are going to be dealt with. We come to this problem with some feeling of frustration, what we call our frustration of federalism. I am not speaking in a partisan way in this connection, but so often I think we give money to the provinces and in order to accept this money they have to share part of the cost. As a result this of course immediately dampens some of their enthusiasm.
Even more important, so often they have to provide the initiative, they have to provide the administration and they really have to provide the pattern by which this legislation that is going to provide physical fitness at the lower levels will be realized. So often there is insufficient direction and planning from the federal government to give this initiative to the provincial governments.
I must say that in many cases I feel this almost circumvents our democratic system. For example, last night we talked about vocational training for unemployed. We find that in spite of the fact that the dominion government has been most generous, this program has not been accepted in the dynamic way in which the federal government itself hoped it would be accepted. The provinces have not gone all out to train unemployed people. This is the problem. When it comes to debating it in this house, of course the government rightly says it is the fault of

the provinces because they have not gone all out in the program. When it is debated in the provinces the provincial governments say it is a federal plan, the federal government has provided 75 per cent of the funds and it is really not their responsibility. I think this is a negation of our whole system of democratic governmental responsibility.
I think the people of Canada tend to become disconcerted by this approach. There is nowhere you can say somebody is at fault or somebody should take the praise for the measure. I hope this will not be the effect of this particular piece of legislation. I hope there will be definite direction and plans from above, and that there will be a real effort to make sure that this legislation is carried out in a dynamic way.
One of the problems that I am sure the provinces are going to face in carrying out this measure is the lack of facilities. It is too bad that last winter we could not have been building recreation centres across Canada into which this program could have fitted. We could have provided the horse before we provided the cart. It is too bad, because I think this is a major problem. The minister mentioned track and field facilities as a major area of our concern. In my constituency there is not an indoor track within 80 miles. How can we, in a climate like ours, produce athletes of Olympic calibre and sports enthusiasts under these conditions? There is not a decent outdoor track for 40 miles, and we virtually have to go down and kick the ponies off the racetrack and try to run the boys and girls in what can only be described as mud in many cases. A country the size of Canada should be providing these facilities at this stage.
We hear this all across Canada from other track and field groups, universities and high schools. Until we provide facilities we cannot produce the results. Is it not too bad that the Minister of Public Works did not announce a bill extending N.H.A. financing to municipalities in order to provide recreation centres, instead of paying out so much money in unemployment insurance. This could be done either through the winter works program or N.H.A. financing, as we have done in providing residences to universities, sewage projects, and so on.
We must show that the national government is serious about this whole matter of physical fitness. We know there is a problem regarding swimming. I think there are only three or four Olympic size swimming pools across this nation. I think this is a serious problem. We are not concerned, I am sure, about simply producing Olympic champions. I am sure when we realize that the U.S.S.R. produced a championship gymnastic team, it

is not the fact that seven of their people won Olympic gold medals which concerns us, but that the Olympic team was chosen from several thousands gymnasts across the U.S.S.R. I am sure this is the kind of thing this legislation is designed to do, and we sincerely hope it will achieve these results. But it must be done with considerable purpose, planning and direction if it is going to provide the kind of results which all of us in this chamber, of every party, are hoping will be achieved.
The second theme, apart from the question of facilities, is the problem of leadership. We still do not have enough people to lead a program of this kind. The central council of physical recreation of Great Britain, which I have just mentioned, set up three national physical recreation centres. Is this not what we need? Perhaps we need national emphasis to provide leadership. That council in Great Britain spent only one fifth the amount we are proposing to spend in one year, and they trained 12,000 people in these recreational centres in every sport imaginable. I think we have to provide leadership, perhaps national physical recreational clinics, to give direction throughout the whole of Canada if this physical fitness program is going to have any effect. It so often happens that plans are arrived at by the national advisory council at the top but they do not come down to the bottom, to the level at which the actual physical fitness takes place. Unless people at the bottom are completely cognizant of those plans at the top and how they are to be carried out, how can a scheme such as this work properly? I think this is a major problem which the former legislation failed to solve.
The Leader of the Opposition mentioned the whole question of financing. We are impressed with the amount of money this government has decided to put into this effort. Perhaps, indeed, it will encourage this government to give more money to the areas of education, the arts and the Canada council. In Britain, for example, 50 per cent of the money is provided by private donations. We want to encourage the people of Canada in this regard, because perhaps this is the answer. The Leader of the Opposition said we do not want voluntary agencies to give up and not contribute anything now and let the national government do it all. Is there not a possibility that private donations to this scheme might have some validity and might be a way of centering the interest of the Canadian people upon this scheme?
Of course the third major aspect of this resolution is the creation of the national advisory council. This is the body which must give the direction at the top. As I see it,
Advisory Council on Sports under the last physical fitness act the problem was that the men at the top knew what they were doing and were making a very worthy effort, but the plans at the top never reached the bottom. I believe this was the major failure of the effort we have already made. I think this is what we must learn from that effort if this program is going to be successful.
The men to be appointed to this council will be a matter of some concern. This will be as large a problem for the minister as deciding which agencies are going to receive the grants. This will be a very difficult problem for the minister and I hope he has already been at work dealing with it. For example, on the council in Great Britain they have men such as Noel Baker, the Nobel prize winner, Right Hon. Vincent Hampden and Brigadier Sir John Hunt. These men are interested in the arts and sciences as well as simply in physical recreation; they are men with wide interests. I think these are the kind of men we want on this council, men who are distinguished in their experience and interests but also who do not see amateur sport simply as poor competition.
I am sure the progress of this bill will be viewed with great interest not only in this house but in the country. I know all of us are hoping that this bill will be worthy of the interest and concern of this chamber, and certainly it will receive the full support of this New Democratic party in this house.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF ADVISORY COUNCIL ON FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the opportunity of speaking on the sports program brought forward by our government to encourage our youth in amateur athletics, and of presenting my personal observations and suggestions in this regard. In my maiden speech in the House of Commons, on January 20, 1959 I was privileged to be the first to mention and support amateur sports and the advisability of the government lending financial assistance in this field. At that time I said:
It is my opinion that it is now time for our government to take a . iok at things. A ministry of sports and athletic uevelopment might be the answer. With government assistance we might be able to reach the day when we could send national teams abroad without forcing their leaders to go begging for funds to make the trip.
Millions of dollars are spent each year on cultural development in this country. I am in total accord with this as any fair minded sportsman would be. I also feel, however, we should spend a similar amount on the physical and athletic development of our young Canadians. Let the government look at the by-product of sports events.
There is the good will the competition fosters for Canada; the easing of international tension through international sports; the raising of the prestige of the country through participation, and the example the sportsmen on these teams set for our youth. So far Canada has not achieved
8726	HOUSE OF
Advisory Council on Sports the place in international competition which the potential we have warrants. However, with proper assistance that goal is attainable.
There were few things in the government's throne speech earlier this session that brought more loud cheers from Canadians, and especially our youth, than the government's announced intention to give financial assistance to the furthering of amateur sport. The position in which I now find myself makes me very happy. For years I, along with many other sports minded Canadians, have been talking up sport, aiding it in every way I can so that young Canadians can develop healthy bodies and healthy minds. I am now in a position to offer suggestions as to how government aid to a national sports program might be administered.
Although we as Canadians become quite smug about our material attainments, our high standard of living, we trail far behind other countries in the provision of facilities for our sportsmen. Russia, of course, is an example which first comes to mind of a country that is leaps and bounds ahead of us. Through a concentrated government crash program, that country has been dotted with sports palaces, swimming pools and local gymnastic training programs. You might say they are as far ahead of us in their programs as their runners were in the summer Olympics at Rome and as their hockey players were in the winter games at Cortina. The results of government assistance like that provided in Russia have been evident in recent Olympic games, just as our lack of a program here has been evident in our dismal showings.
The ideas that I would like now to present are a combination of my own thoughts, and suggestions from other sportsmen across the country that have flowed into me since the announcement that the government would undertake this program of aid to amateur sports. Because we seem so far behind other countries in this matter our problems are manifold, and for that reason they must be approached step by step. I suggest that our three realms of activity could be:
1.	The provision of sports facilities, adequate playing fields, stadia, swimming pools, gymnasiums, tennis courts, and other training and competitive areas. These facilities would mean physical fitness for our youth.
2.	The provision of competent coaches, invaluable to our youth.
3.	Direct financial aid to national teams representing Canada in international events.
To remedy Canada's lack of sports facilities, I suggest that the government consider a plan providing a certain amount of money per year for, say, 20 years. Grants would be


made available to communities which agree to build stadia, playing fields, pools, etc., which conform to recognized international standards, and to any others which Canada may see fit to impose. Because we are far behind, these grants should be substantial so that, say, perhaps 20 communities across the land could get modern facilities each year. These naturally should be strategically located throughout Canada to give the best possible service at the start. The gaps in location could be filled in in future years. This money should not go to communities without there being some evidence of civic support and interest. The government might provide 50 per cent of the cost of any approved scheme; the rest could be raised by the community concerned.
Turning to the question of government aid in the provision of competent coaches for our young sportsmen in every field, it is my suggestion that the government make annual grants to existing amateur sports groups which can come up with a coaching plan and approved coaches who should be, I would think, internationally known figures such as Rocket Richard and Gordie Howe in hockey, Gus Ryder and Cliff Lumsden in swimming, Mr. Reid of Vancouver in rowing, and Wally Brown in track and field, etc. We will have to pay for the best, but if we do it will undoubtedly pay off in a more fit Canada, a healthier youth who will build a healthier nation. The results have been evident in our sister country of the commonwealth, Australia, where a concentrated sports program has produced the world's greatest runners and swimmers.
On the other hand, the government may decide that full time coaches would be desirable. These could be employed by the federal government that will operate the nation's sports program, and made available to clubs across the country on demand. When not out on the hustings in this capacity, these coaches might be planning Canada's future progress in their particular lines, developing visual aids with special films, delivering talks and writing manuals on sport.
Let us now turn to the matter of competition expenses of our sportsmen who will develop this far reaching program. It is my belief and that of millions of sports loving Canadians that all national teams going to international events such as the Olympics, the Pan-American and commonwealth games, world hockey tournaments, Davis cup tennis championships, etc., should have their basic expenses paid by the national treasury. Their costs of uniforms, equipment; hotel and travelling expenses and other incidentals should also be met. I do not believe, however, that

there should be a scheme providing for personal reimbursement for time lost from employment. If some private contributors wished to help defray the loss of money by any individual, that would be another matter. It is my firm belief that all our national sports representatives should be removed from the embarrassing position of having to go, cap in hand, begging for bare necessities when other nations fully back up their sporstmen through the treasury.
I am very close to this problem, coming from the Waterloo North constituency which I call home. Its major municipalities, the twin communities of Kitchener-Waterloo, through their former hockey team, the Dutchmen, represented Canada in two Olympic hockey tournaments. In order to make these two trips the people of Kitchener-Waterloo and the district, along with some sports minded friends, had to raise over $40,000 for expenses. Financial worries for those taking part are a big hindrance in their desire to win. This was clearly demonstrated in the case of the Dutchmen, who had to make a special effort the last few days prior to departure for Squaw Valley in raising extra funds. Yet this team was not representing Kitchener-Waterloo; it was Canada's team. All Canada felt sorrow at their plight and there was experienced almost a national embarrassment when the team lost to the Russians in 1956 and to the Americans last year.
This situation also applied in the cases of Miss Anne Heggtveit, Canada's first Olympic Alpine champion, the champion pair skaters of Toronto and others who competed. They carried the financial burden, assisted by donations from individuals and associations. Our country did not share in the expense incurred in sending these athletes thousands of miles to compete in the highest arena of sports in the world.
In providing this money, however, there is an underlying danger. There must be a proper balance struck so that individual initiative and leadership are maintained and encouraged. Too much welfare dulls the spirit. Not enough of it means misery, as some of our teams that have struggled to compete in international competition will attest. Sport is no different from anything else. If it is made too easy the sportsmen will not appreciate it.
Now the major consideration is, how can this country-wide program of aid to amateur athletics be instituted? This council, to be called a national advisory council on fitness and amateur sport, should have a permanent office in Ottawa, with the funds administered through the department of health and welfare by the minister of that department. So that the ideas can filter down to local
Advisory Council on Sports levels there should be a voluntary provincial council or sports body of some kind headed by an Ottawa appointed sportsman. Then in each sizeable community across the country there should be a local community recreational council similar to the one acting in my home town of Elmira and other similar centres, to carry out the broad program and wishes of the national committee or council. About 15 years ago this council was instituted in my home town and I had the honour and privilege of being its first president. This council has been very successful, and in order to show the committee just what it means, our town of 3,200 people is spending $15,000 every year for recreation and sports purposes.
How can we maintain this spirit of helping while getting aid from the government? One answer could be a national sports day each year, when every local group would sponsor a program to raise money to augment the national effort. We could aim at, perhaps, 10 cents a head. That would provide $10,000 alone in my own twin cities of Kitchener-Waterloo and district, and in Canada as a whole $1.8 million. The money would go a long way to pay administrative costs and some of the expenses. In addition, the publicity and the locally staged efforts would give the program the national focus it would need to whip up country-wide support.
These are my suggestions, Mr. Speaker, for a sports organization that, I believe, will in a few years put Canada in its rightful place in world sports activities, and in so doing it will develop generation after generation of young Canadians with healthy bodies, healthy minds and a true understanding of sportsmanship, fellowship and friendship.
The problem of juvenile delinquency has become so widespread that it constitutes a pretty serious indictment of the society in which we live. The fact that this problem is caused by only a small minority of our youth does not excuse it nor minimize its importance. In 1958 Canada had 31,000 or more juvenile delinquents. Like all proud parents we expect a lot from our children, and we must continue to do so if our young country is to fulfil its ambitions. We should not forget however, that they will only be able to shoulder their responsibilities in a manner consistent with the teaching and example which they have received from us. The sports program suggested by our genial Prime Minister and being brought forward by our government, with the assistance of parents and all sports minded citizens can be priceless in helping to wipe out juvenile delinquency. With a country so young, so virulent, and with such a promising future, can we afford not to have this program?

Advisory Council on Sports
For some years we have had some sports minded citizens who have made a fine contribution to amateur sports, perhaps in some cases unknown to Mr. John Public. I refer to such men as Major Connie Smyth, M.C., of Toronto. Some army officers credit this man with the high place that hockey holds in the army sports program. He made the army hockey conscious when he organized it during world war II. The sports program for Canadian servicemen and their dependents has been steadily broadened in the ten years that Canada has been contributing ground forces directly to NATO. Mr. Len Taylor of Kitchener, one of Ontario's leading sports writers, who has been on many visits to Europe with our competing teams, has this to say:
Some of the most interested people in the projected national sports and recreation council for Canada live in Europe.
Among the Canadian forces overseas there is a greater awareness of the need for a national program than there is among the average man at home. This is due to several factors. One of them is that the army and air force personnel here have been provided with far better facilities than any Canadian community.
Another factor is that they are able to see at first hand what can be done by a national program because most European countries are years ahead of Canada in this field.
These European friends, including our own Canadians, are very interested in the government's sports program aimed at encouraging youth in amateur athletics. May our efforts not be disappointing to them. Recently I read an article written by Peter Fraser in which he refers to another fine Canadian, Mr. Jim Daly, the new national track chairman for the amateur athletic union and former Manitoba half mile champion. This gentleman is promoting a program for more year-round competition on the local level leading up to interprovincial meets and winding up with a national final. Mr. Daly is very enthusiastic and feels that Canada has a track and field potential to finish third in the British empire games. He admits that money is needed to carry out his program, but he feels that sport can ultimately pay its way. This man has done a great deal in promoting track and field for our youth.
Yes, Mr. Chairman, Canada has many such sportsmen ready to take their part in this program. I think of such wonderful organizations as the Royal Canadian Legion. I understand that up to now the Legion has spent up to $80,000 on track and field alone for our young Canadians, and many thousands of dollars on other recreational work. President Kennedy of the United

States recently appointed Charles Wilkinson, the former coach of Oklahoma football teams, to head the national youth fitness program. Mr. Wilkinson thinks that his first problem will be to track down the youth and sell them the idea that getting and staying in shape can be fun. After all, youngsters must be convinced that keeping in condition pays rich, lifelong dividends.
In recent years it has been recognized more and more by Canadians, as well as by our American friends, that physical fitness has an important part to play in the life of every nation; therefore it is gratifying to know that our government has given this desire the impetus it needed, the go-ahead signal that will provide sports for all. I will keep striving to further this program, to assist others in its promotion and to encourage every Canadian to give it his wholehearted support. Let us now forget about our past lack of a national sports program, our lacklustre performances in international events, our poor publicity through weakly supported teams and individual competitors, and look ahead to a brighter future for sports in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, according to press reports which appeared in most Canadian newspapers on August 28 last, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) stated in Toronto on August 26, at the official opening of the international hockey hall of fame, that he would recommend to parliament the establishment of a national sports council to improve conditions in the field of recreation, amateur athletics and physical education.
The resolution we are now considering contains the following recommendations:
1.	The establishment of a national advisory council for the encouragement of fitness and amateur sport.
2.	To provide for the making of grants to agencies, organizations or institutions.
3.	To provide for entering into an agreement with any province for the payment by Canada to the province of certain contributions in respect of the costs of programs relating to fitness and amateur sport.
4.	That the contributions and moneys paid every year do not exceed in the aggregate $5 million.
5.	To provide for the payment of the chairman's remuneration and of the travelling and other expenses of the members of the council-
Mr. Chairman, the resolution has nothing to say about the standards which will establish the statute of an amateur. Will they be the

standards followed for the Olympic games and which are described thus on page 781 of Encyclopaedia Britannica:
(Text):
An amateur is one who participates and always has participated in sport solely for pleasure and for the physical, mental or social benefits he derives therefrom, and to whom participation in sport is nothing more than recreation without material gain, direct or indirect, and in accordance with the rules of the international federation concerned.
The Canadian amateur hockey association has defined an amateur hockey player as follows:
An amateur hockey player is one who either has not engaged or is not engaged in organized professional hockey or, if he is so engaged, has been reinstated.
(Translation):
Is the council considering other standards?
Which groups of amateur athletes will be eligible for government grants?
Mr. Chairman, I should expect that amateur sports which do not draw such large crowds as, let us say, hockey, baseball, basketball, will get the same consideration from the council.
Sports and recreational activities which should get the considerations of the proposed council would be, for instance, swimming, outdoor athletics, track and field events, hockey, boxing, cycling, fencing, gymnastics, physical education, rowing, shooting, archery, tennis, baseball, figure skating, basketball, judo, etc.
Mr. Chairman, the council will have to tackle the difficult task of dividing fairly this money, so that all sports, all organizations and all athletes benefit by it. There lies the problem. And what a problem it will be.
Up to now each group in the field of sports has been looking after itself as best it could. Each leader worked very hard and devotedly to ensure the success of his section. Now, it is to be feared that they will fight one another in an effort to secure the lion's share of this assistance promised by the federal government.
Sports organizations throughout Canada, sports editors and all those interested in the welfare of our youth and in amateur sport, will undoubtedly be invited to offer their suggestions in order that may be found the formula through which sport-and the country -will get the maximum benefit out of that amount of $5 million.
Mr. Chairman, will the council grant bursaries and fellowships to those who would like to become coaches in the sport section of their 90205-6-551
Advisory Council on Sports choice? Will grants be made for the development of regional schools or clinics to train coaches and referees?
Will the council sign agreements with cities and municipalities, through provincial governments, for the construction of recreation halls or gymnasiums? Will the council give assistance to our athletes and teams participating in national games, international games and Olympic games, in the matter, let us say, of transportation, purchasing of equipment, uniforms and even souvenirs?
Mr. Chairman, it is not merely a case of winning victories, there is our country's prestige to think about, the important part the world of sports can play in the improvement of international relations, so that countries may understand one another better.
When the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) referred to those projects, he said:
In 1928, Canada had its best successes at the Olympic games.
I should like also to refer to those who, in 1928, won medals for Canada.
(Text):
Mr. P. Williams in the 100 metre dash, Mr. P. Williams in the 200 metre dash, the Canadian team in the 400 metre relay, E. Catherwood in the high jump and J. Wilson in the 500 metre speed skating. The field in which Canada has the most victories is hockey. World hockey competition started in 1920. Canada won the gold medal in 1920, 1924, 1928 and 1932. In 1936 it was won by Great Britain. In 1940 and 1944 there was no competition because of the war. Canada won in 1948 and 1952. Russia won in 1956 and the United States won in 1960.
