speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my first words, of course, are words of commendation. I should like to thank the Prime Minister for the action which he has taken. I had the opportunity of being in Toronto during the Canadian national exhibition when he made this announcement, which was one of great importance. The amount of $5 million annually is about 83 times the amount which the senior government made available for this purpose last year and is exactly $5 million more than the senior government made available during non-Olympic years. During Olympic years, some $60,000 was made available to the Canadian Olympic association.
I should like also to thank the Minister of National Health and Welfare for the fine presentation he made. He certainly indicated that we do not want a nation of spectators but rather a nation of participants. I was impressed by the words of the Leader of the Opposition. The matters with which he dealt were matters about which I have been concerned for some two or three years. I think the Leader of the Opposition made it clear that this was not entirely a matter which could be brought about solely by assistance from Ottawa. It must begin in the home with encouragement by the national government. I


have been impressed, too, with the work that has been done in this connection for many years by the hon. member for Waterloo North. He has done a great deal to assist amateur sports in this country. I felt, too, that one of the colleagues of the Leader of the Opposition would have introduced a similar resolution years ago had he not passed away while doing the type of thing that he loved, namely trying to stretch a two-bagger into a home run. I am referring to the late Lionel Conacher. I think that had he lived, and had he had the Canada council as a precedent, he would have been encouraged to introduce the type of resolution which has been introduced here today. The resolution and the legislation which will follow it is certainly a step in the right direction. It is noted that within the last year the government of France has made provision for this purpose of $125 million to be spent over the next five years on amateur sport with a view to regaining lost prestige in international competition. The government of Sweden has granted a subsidy to amateur sports bodies of 750,000 pounds. The government of England has been asked to contribute 5 million pounds for revenue expenditure and another 5 million pounds for capital expenditure each year.
In passing may I also thank the many officials from across the country who have been associated with amateur sports bodies for writing to me, my colleagues, the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Health and Welfare, encouraging the type of action that has been introduced in the House of Commons today. The list is too long to refer to all of the organizations and to the many officials who have spent a great deal of time in presenting their valuable suggestions and very learned briefs to persons here in Ottawa. Upon passage of the bill, amateur sport in Canada will enter a new era.
The Leader of the Opposition this morning referred to some of the stars of yesterday. While he did not refer to Percy Williams of Vancouver by name, he made reference indirectly to him. I am sure that all of us will recall that Percy Williams popped the eyeballs out of the sporting world when he won two great events overseas. I am sure most of us will recall that he had great difficulty in making his way first of all to Hamilton and then overseas. His trainer came across Canada escorting Chinese to New York and he made his way overseas behind Percy Williams on a cattle boat. That is the kind of thing that had to go on formerly.
Today amateurs in Canada are facing murderous competition in the world. It is this welcome type of action that is being taken today that will bring about great benefits everywhere. It is the type of resolution

that will affect the masses. A small contribution of say $75 in a small town will do wonders in bringing the "small fry" along. I am sure that in due course we shall be able to uncover "world class" amateur prospects who are at present buried away all over Canada and the nation's morale will benefit from it.
I have what I feel is a practical program following the passage of the bill. The first practical step could be that able, conscientious and qualified people be appointed to the council. This could well be the most important issue because it will be these people who will have so much to do in advising the government and in drafting rules which will in turn help so many people. I therefore suggest to the minister that much time and effort be spent in appointing qualified men from across the country.
I think a very fine job was done in the matter of choosing persons to serve on the Canada council. Generally speaking, I think they have done a very good job. I read the most recent Canada council report. It is a fairly glowing report of the progress that has been made in its field. I should like to feel that after this new council has been appointed and has spent some time on the matter, we shall have from it equally glowing reports. In the last annual Canada council report we find the following statement:
-much has been accomplished. This is clearly true of the support that has been given to the humanities and social sciences. With the assistance that the council has been able to provide, the possibilities for advanced study and research in these two areas have been enormously increased; they have not only been enormously increased, they have been taken advantage of, and productive results have followed.
On another page we find this statement:
The arts story for the year 1960-61 is told in detail elsewhere in this report. Here it is appro-pnate to make the generalization that during the past four years our orchestras, theatres, ballets, opera, art galleries and festivals have all benefited by council support. In this area of the council's responsibility many problems exist but the overall condition is one of growth and often of improvement.
Then the report goes on to refer to the many individuals who have been assisted by the Canada council. I know that when this legislation is passed and the council is appointed, many problems will develop. The council will not be able to cure all the ills that will face amateur sport, but certainly much can be done to minimize and eliminate the major ones.
Another practical suggestion which I should like to make to the minister would be this. Upon appointment of the council I would suggest that the members of it should study closely the operations of the Canada council.
90205-6-551J
Advisory Council on Sports The sports council or council of the other name which the minister has given to this proposed council, will have to decide what amateur sports should be assisted most. The council will have to decide what aid can be given to recreation.
Another practical suggestion I should like to make to the minister would be that members of the council should make a study of what is taking place in other countries and should personally examine the athletic facilities, stadia and so on.
Another suggestion-and in my opinion, this is an extremely important one-is that the council and the government should, at an early date, set up two or three national schools for coaches. Here is a program which could be aimed at the masses and from which, as a natural by-product, our super stars will be developed.
As I indicated, we are entering a new era. The Leader of the Opposition has referred to some of the stars of yesterday. It was said that when Neil Colville first went to New York as an amateur his first account which he submitted to the management was "one sack of apples, one detective story magazine, one pair of shoe laces for dress shoes, one box, small, epsom salts and one telegram to dad." If you compare that account alongside the accounts of modern day stars, it would certainly be refreshing to those who organize amateur sports to go back to that type of thing. In the new era it is no longer good enough for a coach to say, "Here is the net and there is the puck. Put the puck in the net". There is more to the matter than that in this day and generation.
It is no longer true to say, as one athlete said, "Just give me the gloves, any old gloves, and a referee who can count to 10". Times have changed on the world scene, nationally and individually.
I should also like to suggest that the council proclaim an Olympics week every four years, when citizens could be urged to support, with money and otherwise, the Canadian Olympic team. The Leader of the Opposition today pointed out that it was his hope that once the new council was set up and these funds were made available, the public would continue to support our amateurs. Once financial assistance was given to the arts and the humanities, support increased; it did not decrease. I suggest that may well be the situation after we have formed the new council.
I should also like to make another suggestion. Under the new legislation grants should be made to appropriate cities in Canada that show a marked interest in and the ability to hold the Pan-American games.
8732	HOUSE OF
Advisory Council on Sports I am sure hon. members are aware of the fact that Canada has never entertained the Pan-American games. We have never entertained the winter or summer Olympics, or the world hockey finals. It is rather a sad comment to find that next year the world hockey finals go to Colorado.
I hope that in this young and vigorous country we will soon be able to bring these international sports events to Canada, because it will do so much to foster new interest on the part of our young people.
Another suggestion which I put forward is this. May I refer, by way of a good example, to the fact that when Percy Williams returned to Vancouver in 1928 renewed interest was taken in track and field sports, with the result that in Vancouver today we hold the largest track and field meets in all Canada. While Empire stadium is not filled to capacity, the crowds number over 20,000 for these track and field events. I feel that some credit is due to Percy Williams for having set an example.
I should also like to suggest that under this new legislation the federal government should give every consideration to the construction and erection of those things which would encourage the youth of Canada to participate in outdoor activities. That is very significant in my area because we have upwards of 5,000 skiers leaving the province of British Columbia every week to ski at Mount Baker in the United States. I feel that under this legislation encouragement could at least be given to the building of those facilities which will keep our amateurs and our skiers at home. This in itself will reward us in many ways.
With this new fund it will be possible for our outstanding athletes to visit the youth of Canada. Personal visits by our best athletes will do wonders in encouraging others to participate in sport. Knowing the champion pays off with young people.
In the past I have witnessed one soccer club after another coming to Vancouver. This is a fine idea. But very seldom do we see our national amateur hockey clubs on the coast. I hope that with the new funds to be made available we will be able to see our national clubs. Whether it be in hockey, lacrosse, or whatever the sport; and we should see our star tennis players, and so on.
Another suggestion I put forward is that once the new council is formed it could encourage the Department of Trade and Commerce to ensure that Canada constructs hospitality centres at international sports shows. I was impressed with the hospitality centres constructed by France and Austria at Squaw Valley. I should like to suggest


that when winter Olympics are held in Austria next year Canada should construct hospitality centres there. Furthermore, with these new funds we could hand out these simple, inexpensive pins which young people at these events like to wear. This plays a very important part at these shows. We do not lack the common courtesies at these international events, but we are certainly lacking in some of these matters.
I also suggest that the council could encourage the national film board to attend international sports shows to take films of Canadians participating therein. Different organizations across this country would like to secure films of some of these events and see, for instance, some of the figure skating of Barbara Wagner and Bob Paul; but there are no such films available. Here is a job which could be done with the encouragement of the new council. Appropriate training films could be provided and these could be sent across the country.
I should also suggest that when the council is formed they should do everything possible to encourage the C.B.C. to attend these international shows. In the past the C.B.C. radio has been there, but not C.B.C. television. I think a much better job could be done in this regard. I also suggest that sustaining grants be made to various existing sports governing bodies which are organized on a national basis to enable them to do a more effective job of promoting and developing their own particular sport. Another suggestion is that grants of a non-recurring nature should be made for special projects at the national, provincial or local levels.
I should also like to suggest that grants be made to provide necessary salaries for the upgrading of coaches, a matter I touched upon earlier, the initial stage being designed to provide qualified leaders in the universities and colleges. Another suggestion is that grants be made to the Canadian Olympic Association, the British empire and commonwealth games association of Canada and other organizations concerned with officially recognized international events.
Another suggestion I put forward is that grants be made to universities and colleges and other organizations for the encouragement of intersectional games and/or appropriate national championships.
I further suggest that grants be made for the development of suitable programs of physical recreation such as camping, mountaineering, hiking, etc. Furthermore, grants could be made to the Canadian association for health, physical education and recreation to support consultant and leadership services and increased publications.

These are some practical suggestions which I desire to make and I hope that the minister will in due course give consideration to them. In closing, I wish to say once again how pleased I am to find that appropriate action has been taken by this administration. I am sure that in due course the results will be felt everywhere.
I realize that we will not be able to achieve too much in a short period of time. However, I should like to feel that at the next British Empire games Canada will at least rank ahead of South Africa and that in due course at some of these sports events we will be able to get a few more points than Mexico, and the West Indies. I again wish to thank the government for taking this action.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF ADVISORY COUNCIL ON FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the idea of a Canada sports council was in all probability sparked by the success of the Canada council which was established by the Liberal government of Louis St. Laurent to assist the arts, humanities and social sciences. This was a popular move which met great success and has been a tower of strength in assisting worthy individuals and organizations. I venture to say that the general approval which greeted the establishment of the Canada council will also be extended to the Canada sports council.
The Prime Minister's announcement which he made on the occasion of the opening of the hockey hall of fame in Toronto last month, to the effect that a national advisory council on fitness would be established and that an annual federal contribution of $5 million will be made available for the purpose of giving encouragement and stimulation to interest in physical fitness and the development of recreational facilities was received with general approval. It is a recognition that in the day and age in which we live there is a great need for active promotion of sports and athletics on a national basis in which a maximum participation by all those agencies with experience in the field of physical exercise and development should be encouraged.
Here we are dealing with the health and fitness of the people of the nation. I am glad to see in this resolution that the government is concerned with the fitness of the people of the nation. This resolution does not spell out how this sports council will be administered nor who shall benefit most from it. We have agencies such as the Y.M.C.A., scout movements, girl guides, community recreational committees, parks boards, and others, all making an inestimable contribution to the sum total of recreation.
Provincial governments are also doing their share in community sports leadership training. I visualize that the federal government
Advisory Council on Sports sponsored the sports council as a co-ordinator of municipal and provincial governments' efforts in the fitness field, and to meet the opportunities of sending athletes to compete in international contests such as the Olympic games. In such cases, the council would assist in ensuring that no Canadian team would leave our land without maximum training and provisions for their welfare.
We should never allow a situation to arise where a community would bankrupt itself in order to finance its own team as we witnessed when the Belleville hockey team was financed for its attendance at the world competition in Europe a couple of years ago, through a questionable use of city funds, thus casting a shadow on the brilliant victory they won. What was more deplorable was the slander and suspicion of mismanagement directed towards some of that city's elected representatives and faithful servants. I honestly believe that an injustice was done to these public spirited public servants whose sole interest in the matter was to assist in the only way they knew possible to enable their team to win top honours in the international field.
Canada is blessed with a few unselfish hockey enthusiasts who in spite of lack of public support have made a great contribution in fostering the participation of boys of school age in the game of hockey. I have in mind an example in Mr. Maurice Black of Toronto who organized the first hockey school. Out of 70 boys attending only 30 could pay a small tuition fee. If such schools were assisted this would render an inestimable service in the promotion of good clean Canadian sport and at the same time would represent a step forward in assisting Canada to catch up with other countries in terms of athletic achievement and national physical fitness.
The Pepsi-Cola Company of Canada Limited is also to be complimented for its interest and assistance by way of substantial contributions towards enabling some 325,000 young Canadians between ages 12 and 19 to participate in Canadian sport. This was accomplished through the promotion of regional junior championships in a wide range of sports.
Last year, Canada lost the Olympic hockey title at Squaw Valley for the obvious reason that there was a lack of co-ordination in the selection of the team which evidently did not have a sufficient workout in terms of meeting other teams before leaving Canada.
In all of these fields government assistance would be necessary. This loss of prestige by Canada in a sport which was born and developed in this country, revealed without a doubt the need to get the very best out in front before sending a team to an Olympic competition.

Advisory Council on Sports
The loss of the gold medal in the 1960 Olympic hockey event in a sport which we always claimed to be our national game further damaged our prestige and morale. Hockey is to Canada what baseball is to the United States, yet a team from the land of the stars and stripes beat us at our own game.
If as a nation we have grown complacent and are deluding ourselves by thinking that we are superior, and if we are relying on our past performance rather than realizing the ever present danger of being beaten by more determined, better trained, better financed opponents, then we have reached a dangerous state of affairs, and we should not blame the referees but rather our indolent attitude towards amateur sports.
In my opinion the answer to the problem is embodied in the resolution which we are discussing and that is, for the federal government to accept the challenge of encouraging sport in all its phases, and to accept the responsibility of contributing financial support, especially when we are selecting the cream of our youth for international competitions abroad. Canadians are not only proficient in ice hockey, but in skiing, skating, swimming, curling, track and field, rugby and rowing. We have a rowing club in Fort William which won the Lipton trophy in international competition eight years in a row. My constituency also boasts of a rugby team which won the dominion intermediate rugby championship two years ago. In the event that an opportunity of competing in far away places arose, these teams could not enter without a measure of financial support which our city would not be able to provide. The Canadian Legion branches of Manitoba and northwestern Ontario have an Olympic training plan for track and field clubs. In July, 1958 they were able to send some representatives to Toronto. One girl placed first and another second in the high jump event of the Canadian Olympic training plan.
Two summers ago, 11 athletes attended the Canadian Legion youth training course in Toronto, and managed to bring home three gold medals, and several silver and bronze medals. These athletes had to pay their own expenses in attending meets such as the prairie track conference held in Saskatoon, the Pan-American trials, and the invitation meet at Bemidji, Minnesota.
It should be understood that athletes need outside competition for their development without which the chances of winning in a highly competitive sport are almost nil. It is to be noted that the organizations which conduct these various sports activities operate in many ways and are constantly begging

for support. The training and skill required in these sports are sometimes helpful in determining the future of many young men carving out careers for themselves in businesses. Some of these men have gone into businesses of their own, and have made good.
By giving our sports minded young men and women encouragement and assistance in deserving cases we would create a favourable climate for good and intelligent citizenship, resulting in inestimable dividends in terms of service to the nation. The council should not however, consider that its existence is for the sole purpose of assisting athletes to take part in international contests. From the Prime Minister's statement, I gathered that this national advisory council on fitness will function in a pattern similar to the Canada council, and if so, I submit the following suggestions. Qualified leadership, properly trained and highly competent, is priority No. 1. It therefore seems necessary to encourage coaches and physical educators to obtain more training, and money should be provided for clinics and summer courses. Such clinics and courses should include all sports and physical fitness.
I believe that emphasis should be placed on physical fitness with a number of short term courses conducted across Canada, and subsidization should be considered for those who could attend courses of longer duration, even if this involves sending people outside our own country. There is some need for training officials as well as instructors in all the various sports.
I would like to call attention to a matter which should be of special interest to a Canada sports council, and that is the junior leaders training conference which the Y.M.C.A. conducts annually at Geneva park, lake Couchiching, and which was attended to the number of 76, by members of leaders corps this past year, from Saskatoon to Montreal. This is an intensive training program for those who will render volunteer service in their own Y.M.C.A.'s and communities. The cost is carried by the leaders and by their own Y.M.C.A.'s, and if a subsidy in the way of travel were possible, it would mean that more leaders could be brought from outside Ontario. Without enlarging on this, it is obvious that Canada needs more Olympic sized pools and more running tracks. In addition, I feel that every consideration should be given to encourage the family engaging in sports and recreation. I have in mind such things as canoeing, camping, hiking, and such like.
May I presume that the interest of the Canada sports council would be in the amateur and not in the professional athlete. We should,

therefore, have concern for the athlete with a future who does not have the opportunity to go to college or to receive a sports scholarship. I would like to see standards created for sports clubs and athletic organizations, and those meeting the sports standards to be assisted financially so as to involve greater numbers.
Financial aid could be considered for those organizations willing to promote provincial and/or Canadian championships. Finance could be considered for those athletes meeting standards to be assisted to attend provincial and/or Canadian championships.
A general athletic development would contribute to the solution of the problem which faces this young nation of having so many of our young Canadians unfit, as was discovered by medical boards in the second world war to the consternation of Canadians in general. It is worthy of note that Prince Philip, during one of his visits to Canada, brought this national weakness to the attention of the Canadian people in his characteristic and forceful fashion.
What I have been trying to convey is probably not the complete answer. Other hon. members have made notable contributions, particularly the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, who was the first member to bring this to the attention of the government last year. I certainly hope that some of my suggestions may commend themselves to the Prime Minister and to the government. I also hope that during discussion of the bill the government will be willing to accept, if necessary and if found desirable, amendments which may be proposed. I think it will be a great day for Canada and for Canadian youth when we pass this bill and money is made available for worthy individuals and organizations.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, like other members who spoke before me, I am pleased to take this opportunity to say a few words about this resolution.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) announced recently in Toronto that the federal government was going to provide a substantial assistance to the field of amateur sport in Canada. All the young people of Quebec, and even those who are not quite so young, were very enthusiastic when they learned that at long last the central government was going to deal with this matter which, in order of importance, comes immediately after that of primary education. Indeed, sports are an essential complement to the education of our
Advisory Council on Sports youth, and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith) is to be commended for having introduced this measure the results of which will be invaluable in a few years.
On February 10, 1959, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Taylor) made a most eloquent speech in the house-he repeated it this afternoon-when he recommended the establishment of a council to encourage amateur sports. The hon. member must undoubtedly be very happy that the Conservative government has seen fit to take action with respect to his recommendation, which should set an example for all members.
Another member who did a lot to call the government's attention on the importance of setting up an amateur sport council, is the member for Waterloo (Mr. Weichel) who spoke this afternoon but who made numerous speeches in that connection during previous sessions.
The people of the province of Quebec remember that the former premier of our province, the late Maurice Duplessis, liked to attend hockey or baseball games whenever he had the time. It is because of his interest in professional sport that he brought his government to vote-a thing which had never been done before-large amounts of money for the recreational centres of the province, which had been specially established for the practice of amateur sports. His immediate successor, the late Paul Sauve, also recognized the importance of amateur sport and, following the example of his predecessor, contributed much to promote that cause. For example, one of the finest sport centres, the "Centre Paul-Sauve", was erected in Montreal and thousands of young people in the metropolis benefit by it.
In my riding, numerous sport organizations are to be found. In almost all parishes, there is a recreational centre for our youth. Recently, olympiads were held at Vaudreuil and also on Perrot island, where hundreds of young girls and boys took part in the different competitions. The example set by those parishes should prompt all the others to establish such sport festivals. At Hudson, there is the little baseball league, where four clubs are in competition for the local championship. The winning team then plays against other clubs of the area until it is eliminated. We have there some 60 boys between the ages of nine and 13 who are learning, while enjoying themselves, one of the great principles of life: "There is always someone better than you and you must learn how to lose in order to know how to win."

Advisory Council on Sports
I could mention many sport organizations in my county and in the province of Quebec which enable our young citizens to indulge in wholesome recreation and to spend their leisure time building up their bodies and their minds.
I should like to take this opportunity to pay tribute to all voluntary organizers and coaches who are really dedicated and who devote much of their precious time, their efforts and in many cases their money to teach our youth the way to indulge in wholesome recreation.
Sports instructors are doing an invaluable contribution. How many of our youth have been spared from a life of debauch by having been invited to join some amateur team where they have met better companions and found out they had certain natural dispositions which, once developed, restored their confidence and gave them new aspirations? How many of our youth have been lured away from bars by our instructors who made them like sports and showed them how to achieve their physical development?
There are many, many examples, and it is to the credit of those who recognized the importance of amateur sport and who tirelessly worked for that cause. Unfortunately, the number of these charitable people is too limited. Today, in this materialistic age which is affecting all groups of our society, it becomes more and more difficult to ask the individual to make the sacrifice of his time and his energy to teach our youth how to make good use of their leisure hours.
Recreational organizations cannot manage to find the necessary funds to pay for their equipment and provide the locals required by modern sports. Much less can they find the necessary financial means to pay instructors and supervisors who must supplement voluntary workers. Although it is desirable to leave it up to the parents to organize and finance those institutions whose purpose is to supplement the education of their children, it remains that the state, be it at the municipal, provincial or federal level, is duty bound to contribute to the development of amateur sports, which are an indispensable complement to the culture we wish to give our children.
There was a time in the province of Quebec when religious teaching institutions were the only ones to encourage and organize amateur sports. Members of those institutions, priests and teaching brothers, were the only ones to recognize the importance for all young people to practice some kind of sport and to participate in team games.
Those institutions were too widely dispersed in the province of Quebec, and at

that time only a very small proportion of our young people were able to benefit from the advantage of amateur sports.
Today, almost all our villages and parishes have very modern schools and adequate and competent teachers. On the other hand, this lay personnel must be paid according to a contract where the teaching of sports is not mentioned. Therefore, in the very great majority of our schools, more particularly the rural ones, which have known fantastic changes in the last 20 years, organized sports and even the practice of sports are unknown. In our schools, sports are left in the hands of devoted people who do not have enough time to give them the required attention. Our young people therefore suffer from a lack of physical training and competitive spirit which would enable them to face the problems of their age with more confidence.
This is in no way limited to the province of Quebec, but extends to all the rural areas of this country.
This is what an officer of the 4th Canadian brigade meant, when, speaking of relations between the children of our Canadian military personnel stationed in Germany and their young German friends, he said:
(Text):
Canadian kids don't want to play games with their German opposite numbers; the Germans are too athletic and too competitive.
(Translation):
This shows a gap in the sports education of our Canadian youth. We know how Germany recovered politically, economically and morally since the end of the last war, and this is due in a large measure to the physical fitness of all her citizens.
This country which knew the greatest destruction and the worst defeat in her history, in 1945, has rebuilt and is experiencing today a prosperity unequalled by any European country, through the determination and the will to succeed of all her citizens. These two qualities are not hereditary, but are acquired by intensive training from a very tender age. This physical training improves the health and strengthens the will power through participation in competitive sports where there is eagerness to overcome all obstacles.
This example of our young Canadians who refuse to play with their German friends, because they are physically superior, should be a lesson to us.
The measure proposed by the Minister of National Health and Welfare is adequate and will give all the Canadians the required incentive to regain lost time in the field of

amateur sports and will improve their physical condition to make it superior to that of most of their elders.
There is no doubt that the Canadian people love sport. But I think that we are all somewhat of the spectator type sportsmen who prefer to watch their favourite sport while comfortably seated in an arena, or in a chair before a T.Y. set. We would rather watch the performance of some professional hockey or football stars.
I would not wish to criticize our professional athletes who bring us fame, especially in hockey, and who contributed in spreading throughout the world that typically Canadian sport which spotlighted the excellence of our athletes abroad. But our interest in professional sports should not cause confusion in the minds of our youth about the very reason for the existence of sports in a highly civilized country.
Active participation in any sport is becoming more necessary for all young Canadians, particularly so with the modern tendency to replace men by machines, due to which physical effort is becoming less necessary to ensure one's survival.
Since everyone can put forward his suggestions concerning the use of the funds to be voted following the adoption of the legislation before us, I, for one, would rather have greater emphasis placed on youth training in sports and on the practice of physical exercises.
Our young people have no idea of how to organize and amuse themselves until some instructor gives them that knowledge. The young from six to 16 or 18 years of age need a monitor, or a coach to teach them how to participate with enthusiasm in team games. It is also necessary to have someone teach them physical education and other sciences. The participation of our amateur athletes in the Olympics or in other international competitions is very important to maintain our country's prestige abroad, and everyone across Canada is happy whenever one of our fellow citizens wins a trophy or a gold medal for his achievements in a competition. But if we are to increase our achievements in sport competitions abroad, the first thing to do is to train all the young people among whom we shall discover many potential athletes.
I therefore suggest that those monitors and coaches be trained through an agreement with the provinces or by the Canadian armed forces, so that every city, town or parish may have some day, one or more experts in the organization of amateur sports, coaches or physical instructors.
Advisory Council on Sports
A special corps under the control of the Canadian army could be formed and young people 14 years old or more could join during the summer holidays and learn the science of sport organizing and physical education. In addition, when they returned to their books, those young people could teach others what they had learned in such training camps, while they were paid for that service, which would help them to carry on their education.
A number of other suggestions could be made, Mr. Chairman, but what really matters is to arouse, in our young people, the desire to take part in sports and to train themselves so as to become champions, true Canadians, strong and exuberantly healthy.
What young man has not dreamt some day of being as great as Maurice Richard, Gordie Howe, Robert Bedard or Babe Ruth? We must replace this inclination to dreams by the desire to undergo training. We are therefore responsible for giving them the opportunity of doing so and of becoming what we have dreamt of being ourselves one day.
In the resolution, reference is made to the agreements which might be signed with the provinces in order to legislate on the amounts of money to be handed out to them under the physical fitness and amateur sports program. This reference is a good indication of the attitude of the Conservative government-that of always respecting the autonomy of the provinces, especially of those that are very sensitive in that respect, when education is concerned.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I want to say how proud and happy I am to note that the resolution before us will be yet another of the many important accomplishments of this Conservative government. I feel proud, for the benefits which young Canadians will derive from this measure will be to the credit of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and to the credit of all the members of this house, and especially of those who are responsible for it.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a small contribution to this debate. I think that up to the present it has been most useful. The minister put the subject forward on a broad and intelligible basis, and the discussion has been carried forward on that basis. This matter could be of enormous importance. It seems to me that some of the incidental things that have come out during this debate have indicated how important the considerations are. One of the things I liked about the minister's speech was that he made it quite clear this was not merely a resolution on physical fitness
8738	HOUSE OF
Advisory Council on Sports but also on what might be called morale or moral fitness. He pointed out how far-reaching the effect would be, stating that participation in athletics had an effect on peoples' emotional nature; that it helped them make friends. He even suggested it might help us make international friends. He had in mind perhaps an ancient practice which is referred to by one of the nineteenth century poets. In speaking of the Persians he said the Persians taught three useful things: "To draw the bow, to ride and to speak the truth". I take it the implication in that is that they felt physical fitness and moral fitness were akin to each other. I think so too.
I was delighted, as I say, with the breadth of the minister's approach to this subject because I felt that it meant he would be seeking for the national council the kind of men who will understand these things and do a good job.
If I may just digress for a moment, when the minister was speaking about sport being a means to international friendship I thought of the current issue of the London Illustrated News. It was rather pleasant to see a picture of the Russian crew taking the grand challenge at royal Henley and another picture showing an English oarsman winning the singles and being congratulated by the Russian who had been defeated. I am not forgetting what the Leader of the Opposition said this morning, that we need not deceive ourselves when the Russians come to participate in our academic events. They may not be single-minded; they may have other things in their minds, but that does not worry me. My feeling is that in the end it will be good. The more we see of each other, the less likely we are to drop bombs on each other. In my opinion, we must go ahead although there are plenty of discouragements, as the minister implied, with these friendships.
I should like to come back now to say a word about sport and our own parliamentary system. I believe it was the great American writer William James who said the English parliamentary system could not exist without a spirit of sportsmanship. What did he mean by that? I think it is very clear and was made clear by a remark in this house by the late C. D. Howe years ago. He said, speaking of the House of Commons, "we of the government open the house but you in the opposition close it." How true that is. What does that mean? It means that the business of this place could be brought to an absolutely dead end unless there were a spirit of sportsmanship, of give and take.
This same spirit can be applied to other things. It can be applied to business. We know there was a time, perhaps it is not so prevalent now, when a current phrase throughout


the world was, "the word of an Englishman". Consider what a promoter of efficiency that was. We all know that in business if you can take a man at his word, you have greater efficiency. Those of you who are lawyers know that there is a phrase used by lawyers. I would not do business with him on the telephone. We all know what that means. We all know how it slows up the conduct of business.
However, I come back to say that I was glad the minister referred to the emotional side in his speech this morning. Do not let us forget that the Secretary of State for External Affairs, when reviewing external affairs the other day, said that we had to toughen ourselves and be prepared to perhaps make sacrifices and bear burdens we had not borne before. Those of us who have been in the army will know what it would have meant to try to carry on war unless you had people who had been brought up through the practice of sport to have a sporting sense and a spirit of toughness.
I am not going to go into the details of the subject. People who have spoken in this debate know much more than I do about the details of athletics, and they have been able to make much more useful and practical suggestions. There is only one point I want to make, and I want to stress it as strongly as I can. I believe there are a lot of people who regard this bill as something which is designed to promote greater skill and promote a larger number of highly skilled athletes. This is not my idea. I do not mean we should not make a reasonable grant towards the Olympic games. I do not mean that at all. But in my opinion what we want is a democracy of athletics; we want the largest number of people playing. We want them to be playing, as the minister said this morning, not for the prize but for the love of the game.
I was terribly taken aback by what the hon. member for Peterborough said this morning. I could hardly believe my ears. However, I have spoken to him since and I had not misunderstood him. He said we now had in the schools a great many boys who do not want to play games. I assumed every right thinking, healthy Canadian boy wanted to play athletic games. I was devastated to hear that was not so. Then, I began thinking about it and I said to myself, why is it not so? There were two things that occurred to me and I think they are both relevant. The first is professionalism. The production of people of super skill who become heroes to the youth has the effect of discouraging the youth from taking part in games. The boys feel, what is the use; I cannot be an expert so why should I play?

Another thing is the lack of playing fields. I think it was the minister who spoke about city life, automation and the effect of that. When I go up and down my constituency and see boys playing hockey, if you please, on the dry streets without any other place to play, it makes me realize that playing conditions are very unsatisfactory.
I lived in a small city when I was a boy and we had playing fields within 100 yards of my home. We never lacked them. Now, we have this new urban civilization, and I think we are faced with a new problem. I say again that I hope with all my heart the bulk of the grant which is being made will be made to encourage the participation of the largest number. When I was told that the desire to play athletic games had lessened, I wondered if that had anything to do with education. I wondered if the literature the boys were reading was different. We used to read Sir Walter Scott, what I suppose one would call heroic literature. I wondered whether this tendency had disappeared. Those who know more about education than I do will know whether or not this is a consideration.
I feel, with all my heart, that if we are raising a generation of boys who do not like athletic games, then it is a dangerous situation. Every one of us should be concerned about it. I believe that as firmly as I believe that I am standing here. I have little more to add, but I should like to repeat what I said a moment ago. I hope very little of this money will go for the purpose of providing high class coaches and high class players. They will be provided by business. In my opinion the box office will take care of them. But what I hope will come from this legislation is that there will be democracy of athletics and that we shall work against a situation in which young boys sit and watch television or engage in other equally unathletic occupations rather than take part in athletic games.
The last point I wish to make is with regard to the question of the council. It, of course, will be all important. I have no nominations to make. Judging from the minister's speech this morning, I am quite sure that we can safely leave the matter in his hands. I have just one suggestion to make for what it is worth. I believe that the chairman of this council ought to be a man who is in touch with youth. For that reason I would hope the minister would take a good look at universities and other educational institutions, including high schools, if you like. At any rate, I would hope that he would endeavour to find someone who really has been in touch with youth and who knows the problems such
Supply-Health and Welfare as those disclosed this morning by the hon. member for Peterborough. If that is the line on which the grant is used and if that is the line the council follows it seems to me that what we are doing today is something we can look back upon as one of the most important actions we have taken for a long time.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Monteith (Perlh) thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. C-131 to encourage fitness and amateur sport.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this vote of $8 million represents the contributions made by the Department of National Health and Welfare to civil defence. This aspect of civil defence, of course, is confined to emergency health, welfare and training services.
I should like to deal with one aspect of the minister's responsibility. I refer to the two important announcements he made in this house during the course of the last few days, when he advised us of the increase in radioactivity levels following the various explosions, undertaken by the Soviet union, following the breakdown of the nuclear tests talks and the decision of the Soviet union to ignore the moratorium and carry on tests.
Perhaps there is no more important problem facing mankind today than the implications resulting from these explosions. I have already said that the house and the country warmly supports the minister in the decision to keep the Canadian people fully informed of the levels of radiation from these explosions. I sincerely hope the minister will keep up this practice. The country will expect it and will applaud him if from time to time, when parliament is in session or when parliament is not in session, the minister keeps the Canadian people informed about the levels of radiation from test explosions and other forms, more traditional, from which have flowed an even higher measure of radioactivity.
The Leader of the Opposition asked the Prime Minister to see to it that the results of these two recent readings were made known to the United Nations. One would hope that these readings would have an impressive bearing on the proposal now before the United Nations, for a further effort toward banning nuclear tests. However, there are certain aspects of this problem that have not been touched upon in the minister's statements or in the comments made by opposition members following those statements. I think I should deal with these at this time.
I am not quarrelling with what the minister said. Certainly I would not be in any position, scientifically, to take issue with him and I have no doubt that what the minister said represents the best scientific thinking available to him. But since he made these two statements I have had an opportunity of examining the observations made by several Canadian scientists, one in Manitoba and one in Halifax.
I regret that I do not have at my fingertips the names of the two Canadian scientists

who have expressed the view that the levels of radiation, prior to the recent Soviet union explosions did warrant the belief that there was an increase in the danger to human health. The two statements of the minister established the view that the extent of radioactivity in our country, including that brought about by the 13 or 14 Soviet union explosions, had not added appreciably to the danger to human health in our country.
These two scientists, however, take issue with this view. As the minister knows much better than I, the scientific opinion in the world on this whole question is divided. I have before me now some notes that I made on a recent statement of Dr. Linus Pauling, one of the Nobel prize winners in physics. I might possibly have refrained from relying, for the present purposes of my argument, on Dr. Pauling because of the political views which one might reasonably have thought he entertained. However, the recent statement he has made is directed not against any test explosions by the United States-those test explosions, of course, were made underground and in the laboratories-but against the test explosions made by the Soviet union.
I do not believe that if we are going to discharge our responsibility to future generations we can overlook this problem. We need not make dogmatic assertions as to the existing danger, but I do not believe we can ignore the kind of statements made by Dr. Pauling and others.
If future generations should suffer, particularly through strontium 90, which takes a long time to level out, and if as a result of these explosions and other forms of radioactivity human beings suffer from cancer and the like, we in this generation will, I think properly, be held accountable if we do not demonstrate that degree of care and concern which I am sure we all want to display at this time.
Dr. Pauling estimated that today-that is, as of yesterday-the fall-out from nuclear tests carried out by the Soviet union in the current series will increase by 5 per cent to 10 per cent the total of human death and damage which would ultimately have been caused by the tests of all nations up to the end of 1958.
If that statement is true, then the situation is even more serious than that conveyed in the two statements made by the minister. I am sure it will be found that other scientists do not fully agree with these conclusions of Dr. Pauling, but we cannot ignore a man who has been recognized in this field, through having beeen awarded the Nobel prize. We must take into account his views as well as those of Dr. Teller, for instance, the discoverer of the first American atomic bomb.
Supply-Health and Welfare
Dr. Pauling argues that previous tests could be expected to cause, for instance,
140,000	grossly defective children to be born in the next few generations due to the relation of fission products such as cesium 137. He also says that 2 million grossly defective children will be born over hundreds of generations as a result of the atmospheric production of carbon 14, which has a half life of 6,000 years. He also argues that the deaths of 140,000 people before their time in the present and the future generations due to leukaemia, bone cancer, other forms of cancer and other diseases might result from strontium 90 fall-out.
He then points out that if Mr. Khrushchev should carry out his threat of discharging 100 megaton bombs the damage would be double the present calculated damage.
He concludes his statement by saying:
When scientists such as Dr. Edward Teller, the American father of the H-bomb, speaks of there being "no danger" from radioactive fall-out they are using the word "danger" in a special sense. They mean there is no danger of the human race coming to an end or of countries being depopulated by the radioactive fall-out from bomb tests. They do not mean that individual human beings will not suffer and die.
We cannot ignore the deaths and suffering which nuclear testing, certainly if continued on an accelerated scale, will cause. I join with all hon. members of the committee and others in the country, in supporting the government and particularly the Department of National Health and Welfare in the pursuit of the sampling and testing that is being undertaken. We hope it will be possible for countries not now fully contributing to the collective effort of the United Nations in these sampling processes to do so. I believe that Canada is undertaking for certain countries tests on foods such as milk. We hope that in the interests of mankind itself all countries would ultimately assume these responsibilities.
I know the minister is concerned about this problem. He has indicated that thus far there has been no real injury to human health. That was the view taken in the United Kingdom in 1956. The minister might tell us if he subscribes to the view expressed by the Right Hon. Ian Macleod who said on March 22, 1956 that radiation does produce genetic effects but that the radioactivity of the atmosphere is increased only slightly as a result of nuclear bomb explosions. Is the situation today substantially that, notwithstanding the increase in the levels following the recent explosions undertaken by the Soviet union? Is it still the view, as stated by Mr. Macleod at that time, that present knowledge is insufficient to fix precisely the level of radioactivity above which genetic damage would substantially affect the well being of populations?

Supply-Health and Welfare
Mr. Macleod also observed on that occasion that research in genetic changes is necessarily and inevitably slow in producing conclusive results. Have any new conclusions been arrived at with regard to the rapidity from which inferences may be drawn?
Mr. Macleod concluded his statement with remarks which I quoted in the House of Commons in reply to a question put to me in my capacity as minister of national health and welfare. He said, in effect, that it is extremely unlikely that the increase in radioactivity which has appeared up to the present will have any appreciable genetic effect. Since that time there has been increasing evidence unearthed by scientists which would suggest that possibly one cannot now go quite that far. There may not be any evidence to show that the increase in radioactivity will have any appreciable genetic effect, but can one dogmatically say that the increase in radioactivity will not in fact have an appreciable genetic effect?
When the minister replies will he tell us whether or not there has been an expansion of the program under which the University of Toronto is measuring the levels of radiation in the human body and in various substances on the earth's surface? The minister will recall that in 1956 or 1957 the government of that day, with the support of the house, provided a substantial grant to the University of Toronto for the purpose of ensuring a greater measure of reliable information on radiation levels. It would be interesting to know if that work has been extended and if similar work is being done at other universities. I am sure there has been an expansion in this area but I am not familiar with the details. I know that the government has increased the sampling stations and it may be that in that process it has also embarked on an extension of the program through the universities.
This is a matter of the greatest importance. Through the mail we are receiving, there is increasing evidence of public concern over this matter. The government has taken the position as I think have all hon. members that there should be no future nuclear tests. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has been adamant in this particular. He has taken the position that there should be no tests with or without control. That is not the view of all countries, even some in the western world. I believe that the symptoms of the problem and the possible danger arising out of the detonations are such that we cannot be too vigilant in our effort to obtain the most accurate information. If there are grave doubts as to the genetic consequences, then it would seem to me we are in a position in which I would regard


it as immoral to embark on programs of nuclear test explosion, when there is doubt as to the potential danger for the human race.
We are presently engaged and rightly so in expending millions of dollars in research against cancer, one of the great enemies of mankind. We vigorously applaud the achievements of the medical scientists in gradually closing in on that enemy. It would be ironic, if in the face of the progress that has been made, in the light of the resources that are being expended towards that objective, we should through this other medium about which I have been speaking bring about increasing causes of cancer among human beings. I refer not only to cancer but to other forms of illness. Valuable work is being done at the University of Manitoba, I believe, in the examination of milk to ensure that it is free from radioactive forces. About a year ago an assessment was made of an increase in certain Canadian produced milk although it was not said to be a dangerous increase. Scientists hastened to advise us that there was no real danger from the milk tested. The mere fact that in that substance so widely used on this continent there was present even a slight increase was enough to cause great concern.
I need not go on. The minister is aware of this problem. I felt it was incumbent upon me to say these things not in criticism of the government, because it is doing everything I am sure that can reasonably be done in this matter, but to elicit a further statement from the minister.
May I make one further suggestion. The minister's. two statements were correct. In form they observed the objective language of his scientific and professional advisers. It is correct that the most careful use of language should be made in order to give as objective a portrayal as possible; but this language is not always easily understood. It may be, that because of the difficulty of understanding some of the scientific jargon, interpretations are placed on these statements which might be avoided, if greater care were taken not in cheap popularization of these reports but in the use of phrases and words that might give a greater appreciation to the public of the significance of the reports. There was a suggestion in the Ottawa Journal last night along these lines. It struck me that there was some merit in the editorial, and I merely echo it for the minister's consideration.

I want to bring to the attention of the minister a situation which exists in the sales and excise branch which is causing wholesalers a considerable amount of trouble and unnecessary expense. Producers enjoy the privilege of purchasing parts for the repair of machinery used in

Supply-National Revenue production of goods exempt from sales tax simply by making the following declaration on their purchase order:
We hereby certify that the goods purchased and/or imported hereby are to be used directly in the process or manufacture or production of goods.
This privilege is appreciated by producers. However, unlicensed wholesalers are considerably disturbed because they have to purchase goods from suppliers, pay the sales tax and then file a claim later. This is most unfair to wholesalers, and all this trouble could be avoided if the Department of National Revenue would grant the wholesalers permission to use a certificate similar to that which is used by producers to purchase goods from suppliers to fill orders received from producers exempt of sales tax.
I would recommend, therefore, that the regulations be amended to give the same privileges to wholesalers that producers enjoy. I would request also that no one be permitted to make the following declaration on purchase orders without first having obtained approval from the department, together with a certificate number:
We hereby certify that the goods purchased and/or imported hereby are to be used directly in the process or manufacture or production of goods.
If this were done, wholesalers could accept orders and supply the goods exempt of sales tax. At the moment, unlicensed wholesalers receive orders from certain producers who certify that the goods are to be used in production. Some of these producers are not familiar with the regulations and make the aforementioned declaration. The wholesalers accept and execute the order exempt of sales tax, after which they file a claim against the department since the goods were purchased tax included. After verification by the department, some of these claims are rejected. The wholesaler must then send an additional debit note to the producer, sometimes several months after the goods have been supplied. The producer wonders why he gets an additional debit note, enters into discussion with the wholesaler, and quite often refuses to pay because he is under the impression he is entitled to obtain goods exempt of sales tax. In the event such a declaration is erroneously used by a producer, the responsibility is on the wholesaler instead of the department.
In order to avoid this situation, a producer should apply to the department for permission to use the certificate and, upon his application being approved, a serial number should be allotted. Then, the wholesalers would be sure their customers were really entitled to purchase goods exempt of sales

tax. I hope the minister will take this matter up with his officials because I have had a great number of representations from wholesalers and I think the matter is vital to them.

maintopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF ADVISORY COUNCIL ON FITNESS AND AMATEUR SPORT
speechtext:
I should like to bring item 709a of the Customs Tariff to the attention of the minister at this time. Under this item Canadian-made goods can be sent abroad, for example to the United States, and can be admitted duty free on re-entry to Canada within five years provided, among other things, that from the time of the exportation they have not been enhanced in value, improved in condition by the process of manufacture, combined with another article, or treated in some other way.
Otherwise the appropriate duty in full would apply on the re-entry of Canadian goods. I understand that under this section Canadian tires can be sent to the United States and be imported free of duty on new United States trucks and automobiles that are being imported. The words "combined with any other article abroad" preclude expensive Canadian equipment from receiving the minimum of work on it in the United States to combine it for example, with a duty free tractor as an expensive accessory and then being admitted duty free into Canada. The full import duty would then apply because the expensive Canadian equipment had been mounted on a tractor in the United States. If this assembling of equipment was allowed in the United States to some limited degree our working men would have more work and the Canadian would get his finished equipment, in the case that I have in mind, $133 per unit more cheaply.
I can explain this matter by being more explicit in connection with a company. There is, for instance, a John Deere works in Welland under very enterprising and successful management. Their primary product has been farm equipment. It is a subsidiary of the John Deere Company of the United States. They have facilities to manufacture approximately double their present production. At the present time 70 per cent of their production goes to the United States, mostly to New York state and other northeastern states. There is no duty on farm equipment going into the United States or coming into Canada. In the United States this particular company has been diversifying into industrial equipment in recent years. One of their farm equipment plants in the United States has been converted into an industrial equipment plant and facilities have been completed in the United States to turn one of these plants into a tractor plant for the industrial trade.

The Canadian customer has to pay duty on the industrial equipment admitted from the United States but not on the tractor. Two years ago the Canadian plant started to make bulldozers and they sold them in Canada at the same dollar price as that at which they were sold in the United States. The Canadian importer saved the duty. This company is now prepared to spend $40,000 in order to tool up their plant in Welland to make front end loaders; I refer to front end loaders on tractors. They started to do this some time ago but when they became acquainted with item 709a in the tariff act, they were obliged to discontinue it.
These loaders are mounted on crawler tractors in the United States and are imported and the Canadian importer pays duty on them. He pays duty just on the loader. There are approximately $1,500,000 worth of these loaders sold in Canada by this particular company, $1 million worth of them in eastern Canada and about $500,000 worth of them in western Canada.
The company had plans to bring the tractors to Welland for two thirds of their production and to mount Canadian made loaders in Welland. There would be no problem here. They assert that they can make this loader in Welland as cheaply as they can make it in the United States and that the whole unit will sell for the same dollar price in Canada as that in the United States, and that the Canadian buyer would save $133 per unit. The saving, of course, would be in the duty alone.
It is not, however, economical for this company to bring their tractors to Welland, to mount these front end loaders on those tractors there and then ship them to the United States as this would involve extra freight of from $100 to $150, depending on the place to which they were destined in western Canada. The company has no plant in western Canada and it would not pay them to set up the staff and rather expensive equipment for the small volume of business in that part of Canada. If the Canadian equipment could be shipped to the tractor plant in Iowa for their western Canada requirements and then admitted to Canada duty free, the western importers would save $100 as the only extra expense would be the shipping of these particular machines from Welland to Dubuque, Iowa, where they would be mounted on tractors.
As I see it, this company has $1,500,000 worth of business anyhow in Canada in respect of front end loaders. They ship them in from their United States plant and Canadians pay the duty now. Last year I believe Canadian importers paid upwards of $100,000
Supply-National Revenue duty on these particular American made machines. If there were a little bit more flexibility in respect of item 709a so that Canadian manufactured products could be readmitted to Canada, duty free with a maximum allowable amount of work, on them, I think it would help us a great deal with regard to employment here in our country.
The efficient and energetic president at Welland, Mr. D. Brown, obtained permission from his home plant to go ahead with this new manufacture. As I said, he started to tool up and was obliged to discontinue because of section 709a, of which he was not aware. He assumed that these particular machines would be admitted into Canada in much the same way as tires are admitted duty free when they are on United States made trucks and United States made automobiles. If it were possible to go ahead with this project in Canada, they would employ 35 to 40 men steadily on this work. It would provide extra business in Canada. It would help our secondary industries that would be supplying steel. Not only would that be the case, but it would save our importers, on the present basis, upwards of $100,000 in respect of duty. I should like to hear from the minister on this point. I intend to discuss this when the estimates of the Department of Finance are being considered.

If we are getting into that arena, Mr. Chairman, I wish to raise a matter that relates in a close way to this subject. The Minister of National Revenue is of course very familiar with the measures introduced on December 20, 1960 in what was called the baby budget of the Minister of Finance, under which certain resolutions were presented to this house which would amend the Customs Tariff. Supply-National Revenue they would have, under the minister's direction, either a high or a low rate of tariff imposed against them.
It has always been my understanding that from the hour that a budget is introduced, the Department of National Revenue automatically carries into force in its administration the decisions announced on budget night. It is true that we have had some legislative difficulty with respect to some of these items. For example, the other place had not approved, as late as six months after the baby budget was introduced, certain of the proposals of the Minister of Finance. As I say, it has always been my understanding that it is obligatory for the officials of the Department of National Revenue, on the day following the budget, irrespective of whether or not parliament has actually completed the statutory approval, to consider what the Minister of Finance announced in his budget proposals as the law of the land.
I read with some surprise after we recessed during part of July and all of August that the statement had been made that, notwithstanding what the Minister of Finance proposed in his baby budget on December 20, 1960, the officials of the Department of National Revenue had in no instance adhered to the new policy that was part and parcel of what the Minister of Finance proposed in that baby budget.
Whether I agree with it or not, I find this rather surprising. I thought it was completely contradictory of all our practices in the past. I understood that the Minister of National Revenue, associated with the Minister of Finance and the officials of the Department of National Revenue, after a budget proposal is made immediately carries out that policy from the time of the announcement, irrespective of whether or not both houses of parliament have approved of the policy.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Ottawa East raised a question with respect to the administration of the sales tax and its collection as between producers and wholesalers. This is a suggestion which has previously been studied by the department. The whole procedure of the collection of these taxes is under review, of course, at all times. I listened with interest to the suggestion of the hon. member and I can assure him through you, Mr. Chairman, that the department will again take a very close look at this matter and see if in any way and to what extent we might adopt the suggestion proposed by him.
The hon. member for Welland spoke at some length about a problem which is of great interest to him and his constituents and which is of course of interest to Canadians generally; that is, providing the maximum


degree of employment in Canada for Canadians and the working out, in so far as is practical and in so far as the law allows from time to time, co-operation between the productive facilities of the United States and Canada so as to provide maximum employment in Canada.
There are various cases where this has been done to a greater or lesser degree, but the hon. member is referring primarily and specifically to item 709a of the Customs Tariff Act. Of course, whatever my sympathies or feelings may be with respect to this matter, the fact remains that item 709a is part of a taxation statute, and that of course falls within the purview of the Minister of Finance rather than that of the Minister of National Revenue.
It is my responsibility to administer the law as parliament enacts it. Whatever merit there may be in the hon. member's suggestion

and I am not saying there may not be considerable merit in it-it is a matter that parliament must consider on the recommendation of the Minister of Finance, as a fiscal measure. I would hope that when the estimates of the Department of Finance are before the committee-if they have not already been concluded because I am not too sure what progress has been made as I have not been too closely in touch with matters- the hon. member will raise this matter with the Minister of Finance. I can assure him that as far as our department is concerned we will co-operate in every way possible to facilitate the maximum amount of employment for any Canadian industry within the law of this country.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River suggested-and I think correctly-that following the baby budget the departmental officials, or the minister, did not start making decisions with respect to class or kind as set forth in the budget. He suggested this was contrary to the practice which had been followed by the department in former years.
I think there is some misunderstanding here. I am told by officials, and I believe this to be the case, that when the Minister of Finance brings down his budget, any tax changes, reductions or increases automatically come into effect that night regardless of the fact that parliament has not yet approved of them. That is the only way in which we can administer the tax laws of this country, because if there were a long period of time between the announcement of the imposition of a tax or the reduction of a tax business would come to a stop or would be accelerated in certain fields, and so on.
However, I am told this does not apply to legislative changes in principles or in practice, as distinguished from rates. In the

budget speech of the Minister of Finance there were proposals authorizing the minister, then empowered by parliament, to enlarge the scope of the class or kind legislation. Very briefly I may say that was it.
We know that legislation was debated here and it was debated elsewhere. The legislation has not yet received the consent of the Governor General, as I understand it, although I must say that I have received this particular information since I came back. Pending the enactment of this legislation the departmental officials have no authority or power to carry out, nor will they carry out, the principles set forth there with respect to class or kind because they have not the legislative power to do so.
Item agreed to.
