Mr. Chairman, I am curious as is the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate with respect to the administrative action that might have been taken as a result of the changes made in the customs tariff in July or August of 1958. On a former occasion-I think last year when dealing with the estimates-I asked the minister what steps had been taken as a result of the amendments passed in 1958 which altered our law particularly with respect to dumping duties. Perhaps the minister could indicate what administrative decisions have been made by him since that time.
Under protest the minister received discretionary powers as a result of the 1958 amendments. Is he able to tell us what classes of goods have been dealt with since that time under administrative rulings?

I regret, Mr. Chairman, that I do not have clearly in mind what it is the hon. member has reference to but may I point out that the amendments passed in 1958 were fairly substantial and that the department has been administering them constantly since that time. Various rulings and steps have been taken. At one point I did say that no specific action had been taken but to tell the truth I have now forgotten what it was to which I was referring.
I think reference was made to sections 39, 40 and 41 of the act. I can readily put a question on the order paper in order to secure full details.

Mr. Chairman, we all recognize the difficulties under which the minister is labouring and we do not wish to be difficult about this. However, the minister did considerable boasting at one time about the fact that having secured this power, which he told us in 1958 was urgent to the well being of the country, he had never used it but simply held it as a club over the heads of possible importers and kept out goods without any use of it. Surely if the minister has never used the anti-dumping legislation it should not take long to say so.

Supply-National Revenue If he has used it he ought to have in mind in a general way precisely what kind of use has been made of it.

Mr. Chairman, I never boast. I merely make simple assertions of fact. I indignantly deny the suggestion that there was any boasting on the part of the minister. I do remember that at one time I said that I had not exercised certain authority or done certain things under the act. At that time as the hon. member well knew, I was referring to specific powers under the legislation.
Certainly those amendments were essential and under them we have exercised various powers. The hon. member and others said they would operate to the detriment of Canada, would result in tariffs as high as Haman's gallows, and engaged in other speculative comments none of which has been justified by the record.
I remember that I did refer to the section authorizing us to deal with fixed values on fruit and vegetables coming in when the value was below the average for the three year period. When I made that statement we had not taken any action under that particular item. During my recent absence from the office that section has been brought into effect and one declaration was made thereunder, I believe.

Does that relate to
potatoes?

Yes. That is the only step we have taken under that item. There was another matter of values to which I referred at that time. I have forgotten for the moment what it was we were dealing with.
We have taken various steps under section 38 which was amended at that time. There have been questions of having a third-country valuation where goods were coming from a country without a free economy. With respect to the proposed importation of certain goods, as the committee knows, we ordinarily accept the value of the country if it has a free market economy. Where a country has not a free market economy, it is occasionally necessary for the minister to make certain decisions and rulings establishing a third country market value as closely as possible approximating the circumstances in the country of origin. I have done that on several occasions with respect to certain proposed importations of gasoline, certain proposed importations of automobiles, pig iron, textiles and other commodities from countries without a free economy. These come to my mind at once and there may have been others.
Item agreed to.
42. Salaries and other expenses, $331,170.
Mr. Chairman, I assume the minister will have something to say on the subject.

It was not my intention to make any extended remarks. There are various activities of the board to which I could refer. I could deal with the number of hearings the board has held, the amendments to the regulations and applications the board has considered but from time to time these matters have been fairly well reported in the press. The estimates themselves indicate an increase of $32,750 over the amount provided to the board last year. This increase is due almost entirely to the necessity to increase the amount provided for salaries of full-time members of the staff as a result of the general salary revision passed last summer and fall. Just as in the Department of National Revenue, Mr. Chairman, the general salary revision has resulted in some increase in the costs of the operation although there has been no increase in the staff.
In most other objects of expenditure there has been a decrease in the amounts provided this year from last year. That covers the salient features of the board's operations. If there are any questions which the committee wishes me to deal with I shall try to do so.

I wish to make a few observations about an interim decision which was made by the board of broadcast governors after what was described in the press as a closed hearing during recess, on which the board gave a public statement on August 28, about which I made some inquiries of the minister before I had actually seen the statement, and when I had seen only references to it in the press. To make my observations intelligible perhaps I should read the whole of this public announcement made by the board of broadcast governors on August 28 of this year:
At its meeting on Thursday, August 24, the board discussed with representatives of Baton Aldred Rogers Broadcasting Limited, licencee of station CFTO-TV, Toronto, an application passed to the board by the Minister of Transport under section 103(3) of the general regulations pursuant to the Radio Act.
In the highly competitive Toronto market the performance of CFTO-TV compares well with other television stations recently licensed. The programs offered by the station have received commendable audience acceptance, and revenues have met expectations.
I draw the attention of the committee and particularly of the minister to the phrase "and revenues have met expectations" because I think it should be compared with

something I am going to read a little later from these gentlemen. I continue:
The licencee has fully lived up to the commitments made to the board in the provision of facilities and the employment of staff-
I hope the minister is listening to this as well because I intend to read some of these commitments that were made, and if this statement can be reconciled with the statements made by these people to the board at the time of making their application, I have no understanding of the English language.
I go on:
-indeed, expenditures on these and on other operating items, have considerably exceeded the financial commitments of the station.
Whatever that means I do not profess to know.
Additional capital is required-
That is interesting too, as will be seen from something else I intend to read later from the application of these people for this licence.
-and the station should not be unnecessarily delayed-
Mind you, this station came into operation only on January 1 of this year.
-in proceeding with required adjustments.
At the time it came into operation everything was perfectly satisfactory for years ahead. They indeed forecast precisely what their profits would be after a certain period and what their losses would be before that period. This is an extraordinary comment on that forecast.
The board is therefore, announcing the recommendation which has been forwarded to the Minister of Transport.
The board recommends that approval of this application be deferred to provide the applicant an opportunity to receive offers from experienced Canadian broadcasting interests on terms and conditions substantially as favourable to the station as the offer which the applicant has received from the American Broadcasting-Paramount Theatres Incorporated. The board should be advised by noon on September 25-
Which is next Monday.
-of all offers made. If in the opinion of the board, no acceptable offer as defined above has been received by noon on Monday, September 25, the board will at that time recommend the approval of the present application for the transfer of shares. If, in the opinion of the board, an acceptable offer has been received, the board will not recommend the present application and will advise the applicant to submit a new application if he so desires.
Now, sir, in the light of the astounding announcement that apparently something like a quarter of the interest in this Canadian station, which made a particular boast of its Canadian character at the time it made its application, was to be sold to American interests, one should read the application made by the applicant who was successful in getting
Supply-C.B.C.
this licence. I, of course, do not intend to read the whole of it but I should like to read certain selected portions of it, sir, and perhaps make a few comments about it. I have in my hands the transcript of the public hearing held by the B.B.G. on March 14-21, 1960, in the oak room, union station building, Toronto. I turn to page 424. The beginning of the presentation was made on March 17, 1960 by Mr. E. A. Goodman, who I assume was a solicitor representing the applicants. I wish to read from page 425 and a little from 426 a few of the observations he made about the applicant. He cited 12 factors and said:
There can be no doubt that all of the preceding 12 factors must be regarded in the light of this final and all-embracing one.
Now relating this important factor to this hearing, it becomes clear that for the proposed Toronto station to be successful in this very highly competitive area, it is necessary that the licensee possess a wide and varied experience in every field important to television broadcasting, together with the ability to use this experience creatively and imaginatively.
I feel that our presentation this morning will substantiate that Baton Aldred Rogers Limited possesses the financial resources-
I ask the minister to note this:
-possesses the financial resources, the material resources, but above all, the human resources that fully qualify them for the privilege and responsibility that the holding of this public franchise entails.
Now the presentation will take place in four phases. The first phase covers the human aspect, it deals with the people presently associated with or to be employed by this company; the second phase covers the financial aspect, that is the capital that is available from its expenditure; the third phase sets forth the technical details,-
I am not going to go on with that.
-and the fourth and final phase, which is a culmination of everything else, covers programming.
The first and second are the two I am going to deal with, and I am going to read a few points relative to the point made. On page 427 we find the following:
Now I turn to the first phase of our presentation, the human aspect. The people responsible for its management are the most important factor in any company. This is particularly true when you are in a creative field like television concerned with education, the dissemination of information and the presentation of entertainment.
Then, he goes on to describe very briefly who these people are. The principal one is Mr. John Bassett, who is the chairman of the board of the company and who has a connection also, of course, with a newspaper known as the Toronto Telegram. He explained Mr. Bassett's connection with the Telegram and various other philanthropic activities- I use that term advisedly. Then, he went on to say:
Mr. Bassett, however, possesses qualities which are even more important to the operation of the

Supply-C.B.C.
proposed station than his newspaper and executive experience. These are a deep understanding of and a high regard for his fellow men.
I am sure, sir, that the board was particularly touched by that observation. Mr. Bassett was then given the task of presenting his colleagues. He pointed out how difficult it was going to be for this station to compete with the three stations in Buffalo and with the C.B.C. and to build up an audience with programs that were essentially Canadian in content. He saw the Toronto station as an anchor to the whole of private television broadcasting in Canada outside the national network. He said, as found on page 429:
It is our belief that none of these requirements will be met, nor will the job of building a station be successful, if the new television station is simply to be a carbon copy in concept and programming of the American stations which now come so strongly into this area.
I hope the minister has noted the words, "a carbon copy", since now they are proposing to turn the station over for all practical purposes to the American Broadcasting Company.
To meet these problems it has been necessary, we believe-
Will the minister note this particularly.
-to build a company in which each shareholder has a specific duty in management and in which each member of the management group has a definite responsibility and a particular contribution to make.
In other words, this was a package and the whole package had been very carefully put together to be the best broadcasting station in Canada.
This we have tried to do. We have no investors in the sense that there is absentee ownership.
That was one of the great things, "no investors in the sense that there is absentee ownership". Then he goes on to talk about the importance of the local character of the company and so on. As found on page 430, he said:
In order to achieve these objectives we believed that it was necessary to try to build a company where those responsible for management and direction would have an intimate and lively knowledge of the local conditions in Toronto...
Such, of course, as would obviously be possessed by the American Broadcasting Company. Then he goes on:
I am sure the members of the board have noted in our original brief that 51 per cent of the voting stock of Baton Aldred Rogers is controlled by the Toronto Telegram, although our financial participation in the profits which may be derived from this operation is limited to 40 per cent. In this way control of the company is vested with the Telegram, and I may say to the board this organization was done deliberately because it was our belief that responsibility and control go hand in hand.
I must say that that particular point made by Mr. Bassett seems to have been clearly

emphasized by some of the events that have taken place since, and if the minister wants any confirmation perhaps he might like to consult Mr. Aldred or some of the other people now being pushed out. Mr. Bassett went on to say on the next page:
... therefore, through mutual agreement among all the shareholders of Baton Aldred Rogers it has been decided to vest control with the Telegram as we believe this institution has developed over the years a recognized concept of Canadian public service. It is our belief that through this concept, plus the extra invaluable assistance that the newspaper can give us in designing our seven daily news broadcasts, we have followed the proper course and one which is designed to ensure both the ultimate success of the station and the development of television in Toronto on the broadest possible Canadian base.
Then, on page 432 he said:
The president of the company-
Who is no longer going to be there under this new set-up.
-Mr. Aldred, has a wealth of practical experience in all phases of broadcasting and he, of course, will devote his entire working time to Baton Aldred Rogers.
Then he has something to say about Mr. Foster Hewitt, Mr. Ted Rogers, Mr. Nathan-son and Mr. Purdy, the program director who is no longer program director. Then he goes on to point out how important to the whole scheme of this station Mr. Aldred and Mr. Purdy are. He says:
For this reason it is essential, we believe, that programming plans are completed on a sound basis before the station ever goes on the air. This Mr. Aldred and Mr. Purdy have done, and it is our belief that largely through their efforts we will be able to hold a great proportion of the new audience who are awaiting the advent of channel 9 in the Toronto area.
Mr. Bassett only took nine months or even less, actually about six months, to change his mind apparently about the merits of these gentlemen. Then he goes on to point out what a great job the station is going to do in the French language. I am not going to say anything about that. Perhaps it would be just as well not to, but I draw attention to this paragraph on page 435:
I have covered these points, Mr. Chairman, ladies and gentlemen, to try and indicate that every shareholder of Baton Aldred Rogers and every member of our management group, as well as our board of directors, have been chosen specifically because of some particular talent and experience that we believe is essential for the development of a successful television station in Toronto.
Now they are going to be replaced, except Mr. Bassett, by the American Broadcasting Company. Then he goes on:
We recognize that there is certainly no place in Canada where a more competitive situation exists and, if this station is to be successful, not only commercially but as a means of developing among Canadian viewers an appreciation

of Canadian talent, Canadian programs and a greater understanding of Canadian events and the effect those events have on their own lives, then those who are charged with the responsibility of station management and development, we believe, must also be directly and personally concerned through ownership.
That ownership is now to be transferred to the American Broadcasting Company. Then there is a lot more in the same vein, quite a good deal of it in French, and then Mr. Bassett goes on to sum up and says, as found on page 440:
. .. the character of our company, we believe, is completely Canadian and essentially local.
Essentially local. The American Broadcasting Company.
I do not mean "local" in a narrow parochial sense.
Evidently not.
Indeed our program director, Mr. Purdy, as I have told you, has had a very broad experience in this field here, in the United Kingdom and in the United States.
Now he is apparently going to have more experience somewhere else.
Mr. Aldred, our president, is perhaps one of the best known men in television in North America.
He is also going to be one of the best known somewhere else than in Toronto.
But I do mean that this is a group of Toronto men who believe that a Toronto television station can only be successful in every sense of the word if those charged with the responsibility of management are extremely sensitive to the needs-
I do not think the board thought at that time that Mr. Bassett meant financial needs.
-the wishes and the aspirations of the viewing audience within our own area here.
Anything that could be more of a travesty than that in the face of the application which the board has now decided to grant, unless some philanthropic Canadian comes along to subsidize Mr. Bassett and leave him with 51 per cent control, it would be pretty hard to find. Then, listen to this:
We believe that the responsibility of management must be completely interwoven with the responsibility of ownership.
Does he still believe that? If he does, that means that the American Broadcasting Company is going to have a pretty big say in management. I repeat:
We believe that the responsibility of management must be completely interwoven with the responsibility of ownership so that the success or otherwise of this station will be reflected directly by the ability and effort of the individuals who hold these positions. Within our group of ownership and management we have built a team-.
I stress that word, sir, "a team".
-thoroughly experienced and trained in the whole field of mass communications as represented by newspapers, films, radio and television. This has been done deliberately because it is our belief that only this kind of team-

I stress that, only this kind of team, and not one word about the American Broadcasting Company or Paramount Theatres.
-working together with a common interest in the public good, can ensure the ultimate success of this new television station.
I felt, then, that was really all I intended to read until I turned to page 513. Then, I did feel I should read the beginning of page 513 because, in a way, perhaps it is rather prophetic. I quote:

Yes, Mr. Haig. You can conclude that. We have gone a good deal along the way, as you can see, by establishing a nucleus-
Then, in brackets and in capital letters I find this:
(All lights in building go out and the answer given by Mr. Bassett was not recorded).
Well, Mr. Bassett was not satisfied with just putting the lights out. He appeared again the next day and, in reply and in a very-condescending fashion indeed, he congratulated all the other applicants on the applications that they had made. One could make some comment on that, but I think it will be in everyone's mind so I will refrain from making it.
Then he said this, as reported at page 986:
We believe that the most important part of the character of Baton Aldred Rogers Broadcasting Limited is that all its shareholders have a direct responsibility in management, and that these shareholders, all Torontonians, came together deliberately because it was our belief that we had a specific contribution to make to the success of television in the Toronto area. The shareholders are all interwoven into management, and in this sense they have direct responsibility and there are no such things as absentee shareholders.
It almost looks as though Mr. Bassett was anticipating something and trying to guard against it even then. I continue the quotation:
Each of our directors has proven business and professional experience. We believe that this station, to be successful in such a competitive market, that executive ability and experience are required in addition to the direct experience of the creating and performing arts. Our board of directors, with every shareholder represented on it, and participating daily in the operation of this station, does have those requirements.
Then, a little later on, on the same page, I find this:
In our main presentation we dealt at length with the financial aspect of our proposed station. I don't wish to go into it again. I just wish to make the one observation. That after providing for our pre-operating losses and for what we think to be an adequate operating capital, we have provided for a cash contingency of $1 million to meet some of the difficulties which all the applicants have spoken about in the early days of operation ...
We have provided that there will be no repayment to shareholders at all in the first five years of our operation. We have provided for this financing from our own shareholders and without setting up through this company any bank loans.

Supply-C.B.C.
In other words, Mr. Bassett certainly gave the board every reason to feel that the financial basis of this company, the financial basis of this operation, was quite adequate. I am sure that the board, notwithstanding the pressures which one cannot help but feel were upon the board and about which I have had something to say on other occasions, would not have granted this licence if they had believed that six months later Mr. Bassett would be back telling them he was in financial difficulties, and telling them that this closely interwoven group that was going to make this the best Canadian television station had disintegrated for reasons which we do not know; that these great and talented Canadians no longer seemed to have the talent required and that in order to rescue this financially precarious operation the American Broadcasting Company would have to be brought in.
It is apparently true that the hearings were in private and all one can learn about what really went on is from reading what Mr. Bassett calls the competitive press in Toronto. I must say that after reading the different articles in the different Toronto newspapers one gets rather different views of what the real situation is. It does seem to me in the circumstances to be rather extraordinary, in view of the assurances given the board, that this hearing should have been held in private at all. What is more extraordinary than that is that the board would consider for one minute permitting this minority stock ownership to be transferred to these United States interests. If there was one thing that was made clearer than any other on both sides of the house, and by no one more eloquently than the present minister, it was that the whole purpose of public participation in broadcasting, public control and regulation of broadcasting, was to keep it Canadian. No one thinks that the American Broadcasting Company and Paramount Theatres are a group of philanthropists. If they are going into this operation, they are going into it to make money, and not just to make money out of the televising of their programs. No doubt, they hope to make money by selling their product to the station. It may well be that from a purely technical standpoint, they will have a better product to offer than the one made at home. But to have the home made product is the reason we have any public broadcasting in Canada at all.
It is precisely because we were afraid the whole market would have been taken by United States interests if there had not been public participation, that we have this public participation. I have never heard any Canadian who was not a socialist defend it on any other grounds. I have never defended

it on any other grounds. I think it would be far better, if we could have the assurance that the broadcasting would be Canadian, to have entirely private broadcasting. But regardless of party most of us in this country, from the days of the Aird report and the days when Mr. Bennett brought in the legislation to establish the radio commission and the days when Mr. Howe introduced the C.B.C., have felt that the only way we could have control over broadcasting in this country was to have public participation in it and pretty rigid public control. It is for this reason we have this participation and this control which, though it has varied a good deal in detail to meet new conditions, has been fundamentally the same ever since the parliament of this country enacted the first legislation in the early thirties.
I say, sir, that we recall only a few short months ago in 1960 when these applications were heard that there were nine applicants for the T.V. station in Toronto. Three of these applicants were closely associated with and almost indistinguishable from the three newspapers. I have said on several occasions that I thought the board should have rejected these applications out of hand from all three newspapers on the ground that where it was possible to have equally good operations unconnected with newspapers, that was to be preferred. I have also said that there are many places in Canada, and I could document these at length but I am not going to do so now, where there is no one except a newspaper or its publisher willing to risk money in the television field. Where that situation arises, people should not be denied television nor should the taxpayers be forced to build a station just because that condition exists.
However, this was not the condition in Toronto. There were six other applications and the board described the applications as all of excellent quality. There were six other applicants who could have been considered if these three applicants had been, as I maintain they should have been in the light of the debates that took place in parliament when the board of broadcast governors was set up, thrown out before the hearings were even held. Only the other six should have been considered. I am seeking, sir, not to go into the realm of rumour and speculation to which reference has been made or to refer to the exchange I had with the chairman of the board of broadcast governors in the special committee.
However this company may have obtained this licence in the first place, the fact is that it obtained it; and surely it should be expected either to live up to the terms under which it obtained that licence or to lose the licence and not to have a United

States company brought to the rescue. My suggestion is this, Mr. Chairman: If they cannot get suitable Canadian participants by the deadline on Monday I suggest that, far from approving this proposal, what the board should do is to call for new applications for that station and to apply to that station the provisions of the Canadian Broadcasting Act as it was prior to the recent broadcasting legislation which was put into effect and to say that the new applicant would be obliged to reimburse the existing owners for all their out-of-pocket expenditures properly depreciated so that they would not be robbed in any way.
However, here they have been given a piece of the public domain on representations-some of which I read-which they have clearly not lived up to and now it is proposed to allow a United States company-and I may say, a very reputable company-to come in and rescue them financially. We even read that it is far more than the stock that is being bought and that this company is also paying off their debts. I do not believe there are many Canadians who think for one minute that a company is going to do that sort of thing in order to have a minority interest as an investment in an outfit which claimed to be financially solvent when it made its application and which six months after going into operation has to be rescued financially in this way.
I say that this is a scandalous proposal made by the board of broadcast governors and that if they persist in this proposal Her Majesty's ministers should not entertain their recommendation for one instant as it would be utterly contrary to everything that they have professed to believe in, or everything that was professed by the minister when he introduced the legislation in 1958, and contrary to all the principles on which all of us have believed public broadcasting stood in this country.
I say that there might be another solution of this matter. There were these other six applicants. It might be that Mr. Bassett could now be satisfied with a minority interest and that one of these other applicants could take over a majority or controlling interest.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I was saying that there might be another solution of this problem. In view of all the circumstances I would not think that there would be any great likelihood of any new applicant arising apart from those who made applications in 1960. Knowing a little bit of subsequent history, I doubt that one of those applicants would be very apt to apply or, if he did so, that he would be very apt to qualify inasmuch as that gentleman has since gone to the United States, I believe, and has sought to accelerate his acceptance as a United States citizen. But let us consider certain other applicants.
There is one very distinguished applicant who is not a political friend of mine. At least he was closely associated with one of the applications. I refer to Mr. Sedgwick. Mr. Sedgwick and his family have had a long experience in the broadcasting business. As I say, while I do not share his political views, I have a good deal of respect for his capacities in many directions. I cannot imagine Mr. Sedgwick or his associates coming along for one minute and accepting this suggestion of the B.B.G. that they should accept a minority interest in the station, with Mr. John Bassett, who has already fired all his previous associates, standing there with a club ready to club him. I would not think that any Canadian applicant would come in under those terms. However, I suggest that those are not the only terms.
I suggest that this is an applicant who has failed to carry out his undertaking, and who has made a mess of this thing financially. I am not saying anything about its programs.

Supply-C.B.C.
I do not know anything about them. I do not happen to live in Toronto. To the best of my knowledge, I have never seen any of its broadcasts. They may be just as good as the B.B.G. said they were. I hope they are. But what I am saying is that they appear to have made a financial mess of this venture. I think they were quite right in saying that it would be a tough problem to run a private television station in this highly competitive market. However, because they have shown that they are not competent to do it effectively, I say that is no reason why, because some Canadian is not, for a minority interest, ready to come in and bail them out, we should allow Americans to do it, particularly the American Broadcasting Company.
One cannot help but feel that this is a backdoor method of establishing what in effect is bound increasingly to become merely another affiliate, perhaps with a little arrangement here and there to meet the exigencies of the laws and regulations, of one of the United States chains. If that is what we had wanted for our private stations in Canada, we would not need to be spending any money on the board of broadcast governors or on the C.B.C.
I say that this proposition is something that should simply be rejected. I think it should have been rejected out of hand by the board of broadcast governors. I cannot understand what possible defence there can be for their decision. I do not expect the minister to defend their decision. The minister has pointed out over and over again that he does not seek to influence their decisions. However, that does not exempt them from the criticism of this parliament to which they are responsible. It does not, of course, remove from us our right to criticize their conduct in this particular, as I am doing now.
The board of broadcast governors, of course, cannot make the final decision about this matter. All they can do is to make a recommendation. The final decision must be made by the governor in council. Hence the government itself cannot escape its responsibility in this matter and it should not seek to do so. It seems to me that we in this parliament should now indicate our views about this transaction so that the board of broadcast governors may be aware of them, in the hope that some different solution to this problem may be found.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall vote 42 carry?

Before this vote carries, Mr. Chairman, possibly the minister could give the information which was asked for and which he said he would give me at a later date, when I asked him a question about the application of the Rimouski station for the

erection of a satellite station to serve Madawaska and Victoria counties in New Brunswick.
I understand that the board of broadcast governors has approved the application, which was heard on February 24 of this year. That is almost seven months ago. The population of Madawaska and Victoria are still awaiting the service for which they have been asking for many months. I understand that the reason for the delay is that the Department of Transport has not granted the licence which has been approved by the board of broadcast governors. I wonder whether the minister would comment on this application.

Mr. Chairman, the facts of this situation are that the order in council has been passed and it has been published. That was done several days ago. I have forgotten the exact date.
I did not deal with the arguments of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate because, frankly, I doubt whether they are in order and I do not propose to become involved in a discussion about something which the board has considered and has adjourned to a future date.
If and when decisions are brought down and action is taken I think that would be the proper time to deal with the matter, but I do not think I should comment on it at the moment. In my opinion, as far as I am concerned this matter is sub judice and is something upon which I should not comment at all.
I do not want to be taken as agreeing with many of the statements which have been made, despite the fact that they attracted the hilarity of representatives of certain newspapers which apparently appreciated them. I must say it is the greatest tribute that could be paid to the board of broadcast governors- I am not assuming, but I am hoping this is the conclusion of this debate-that after a year of strenuous activity in which they have had so much responsibility, criticism has centred on this one situation, which is something that has not yet been finalized.

Mr. Chairman, I think perhaps the minister would have been wiser not to have offered the temptation which he offered in his last sentence or two, because I have a whole file of things, some of which I raised at the committee, that I would like to say about the work of the board of broadcast governors. However, I recognize that there will be plenty of time to do this in another session, which I hope will not be the longest session in the history of the Canadian parliament since confederation.
You will make this a shorter one if we can get through this item.

I advise the minister that if he wants to get through this item he should listen to what I am saying. I was saying, when my sentence was cut in two by the minister's intervention, that I deliberately did not intend to mention any other matter because it did not seem to me there was any other matter that was so urgent that it could not be considered at what 1 feel would be a more opportune time.
However, I did feel that this matter, since apparently it is going to be settled on Monday next, is so urgent that any opposition member of this house, and indeed any hon. member of this house feeling as I do, would have been derelict in his duty not to see that it was aired. I also agree with the minister, that in the position in which he finds himself, as a member of the cabinet which will sooner or later have to reach a final determination about the matter-which, as he properly says, is not yet final-he has taken the right course in making no comment upon my observations.
I must say that I was rather encouraged the other day, and I noticed the Telegram was correspondingly discouraged, when the minister suggested that when I in very brief form expressed the same sentiments I was probably expressing sentiments widely held throughout the house.
I am not going to seek a denial or anything else from the minister, but I should like to go on believing that the views I have expressed are not very different from the real views of the Minister of National Revenue.
Item agreed to.
43.	Grant in respect of the net operating requirements of the radio and television services, $70,418,000.

Mr. Chairman, I assume from the indications which have been given to the house by the Minister of Veterans Affairs in his capacity of house leader that no one has any intention at this session of arranging for a debate on the report of the committee on broadcasting. I fervently hope that my interpretation of the views of the house leader is a correct one.
I would hope so.

I simply wanted to say, so that it would be on the record, and I think I can probably do it between now and six o'clock, that speaking not just for myself but for the Liberal party, I dissent and we dissent from the recommendation made with respect to the proposed recomposition of the
Supply-C.B.C.
board of directors of the C.B.C., and particularly to the recommendation that no executive officer or other employee of the corporation shall be a director of the corporation. The reasons for this dissent will be very plain from the debates of 1958, and our position in this regard has been strengthened rather than weakened by the experience since.
I felt it was desirable to say this because I do hope that if the government should decide between now and the next session to bring in any legislation to amend the Broadcasting Act, they will not bring in legislation which will create a board of political appointees solely and exclude from that board the officers of long experience who are now, respectively, the president and the vice president of the corporation.
Mr. Chairman, where was the hon. member when the report was written?
Mr. Chairman, I am very glad the hon. member for St. John's East asked that question.
Six o'clock.

When the report was written the hon. member who is now speaking was in his place in this house, which was sitting at the same time as the committee was meeting, as has happened over and over in this longest of all sessions because of the shocking mismanagement of the business of the house by the government.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall vote 43 carry?

I see the clock, Mr. Chairman. Of course, we are all so pleased that the minister is in such good health again. I am only going to say that he knows I have had a long-standing interest with respect to the possibility of the C.B.C. doing something for Atikokan, Fort Frances, the Red lake area and some other parts of that very large riding which I represent. I do not expect a reply from the minister tonight. I would simply ask him, in view of his ability to be back on the job, to look at this matter again and perhaps advise me and my constituents about it.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall vote 43 carry?

Mr. Chairman, before this vote carries I should just like to say one word. 1 am not going to oppose the carrying of the vote right now. However, I would like to make it very clear that there are two considerations in the minds of the opposition in agreeing to the carrying of this vote. One is a proper human concern for the Minister of National Revenue, for whom we have great respect. I do not say that in any patronizing way at all; we realize that the minister is carrying a very heavy load-

Business of the House
Hear, hear.

-under considerable difficulties. The second reason is that the session has already been so prolonged. But we do hope that in taking this position-and I am speaking here, I think, for hon. members on both sides of the house-we will not read in half the newspapers in the country tomorrow that, notwithstanding the shocking increase in the cost of the C.B.C., parliament dealt with the item in 10 minutes. After all, we did not deal with it in ten minutes; we spent many days on it in the special committee. Even the Ottawa Journal said editorially the other day that we ought to give the C.B.C. a rest because parliament had spent so much time dealing with its affairs.
Item agreed to.

At the conclusion of these items, Mr. Chairman, I wish to express my appreciation to the committee and make it plain that I hope it is not out of consideration for myself that their scrutiny has been expedited, because the minister could sit here tomorrow and deal with these matters. However, I thought if we got through with them tonight we might facilitate business tomorrow.
Resolutions adopted in committee of supply this day reported and concurred in.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I take it we will be sitting tomorrow. In view of that I would ask the house leader to tell us what business we will take tomorrow. Perhaps he will also indicate what we will be doing next week.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the nouse for the commendable progress it made today. We will take the estimates of privy council first tomorrow followed by those of
veterans affairs and those under the heading of legislation. There are some additional supplementary estimates which we shall endeavour to clear away. If time permits and the house is willing we might take the estimates of the Department of Finance.
Tomorrow I shall be better able to forecast the completion of the business of this session and make a good guess about the termination, with the assistance of the opposition.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I direct the minister's attention to the fact that on my list there are several small items such as insurance and Auditor General which must be dealt with.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not wish to hurry the house but those could be taken tomorrow. They normally are taken following the estimates of the Department of Finance.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would hope that we could dispose of all these smaller items with the exception of finance. If the minister calls finance tomorrow there will be a general debate. Could we leave that until next week?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I take it that these other items might be called in advance of the Department of Finance.
They are not under the heading "Finance" in the book.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
No, but they are normally dealt with following the estimates of finance. We could call Auditor General, atomic energy, national research, insurance and governor general which follows privy council. The intention for tomorrow would be to complete the items I mentioned with the possible exception of the Department of Finance. I am not pressing the matter at all.
It being 6.06 p.m., the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
